#2859. 5 Qs, 5 As: Washington fans ‘hate’ the name Commanders

The Washington football team (not to be confused with the Washington Football Team) is on their fifth season of being named the Commanders. And it sounds as though fans of the team are no bigger fans of "Commanders" today than they were in 2022. In fact, the longer they go into the name change, the more they might want to change it again.

It's hard for me to imagine or accept that there is a team in the NFL named the "Commanders", which still feels like a made-up name for a fictional pro football league in a Keanu Reeves or Kevin Costner movie.

Even so, this is the name that they're stuck with today, and it is the team that the Los Angeles Rams will face on Sunday in a critical moment for both franchises:

If the Rams lose, all hell could break loose before the trade deadline Tuesday.

If the Commanders lose, head coach Dan Quinn may not be associated with the "football team" by Monday.

Washington is 2-4-1 and seeking their second win in a row since the return of quarterback Jayden Daniels. To get to know them — and their Football Team Fans — better, I sent five questions to Andrew Y at Hogs Haven. He sent me back five answers.

Q: The Commanders don't have a player in the top-30 for rushing yards or the top-60 for receiving yards. I feel like that would be very disappointing for fans, to not have one skill player so far this season who you can at least look forward to watching, win or lose. But those are stats, not necessarily reality. Who is the one healthy skill player on the team who Washington fans can look forward to watching each week?

A: I think the player most Commanders fans would point to is rookie WR and 3rd-round pick Antonio Williams. He's shown tremendous route-running nuance and short-area quickness to get open in the middle field and has been a consistent target getter, with 23 catches for 259 yards so far this season. Those simple stats don't rely do credit to his ability though, as he's generated a 96.7 passer rating when targeted and is PFF's second-highest graded rookie receiver. Dan Quinn made clear that with the loss of Terry McLaurin, he expects Antonio Williams' role to increase the most and indeed Williams led all receivers in snaps and routes last week against the Eagles.

Q: Five years in, how is the name "Commanders" sitting with fans? Do you ever long for the days of Football Team again?

A: Honestly, I think most fans hate the name Commanders. It's the last stinky gift given to us by former owner Dan Snyder that the new leadership hasn't been able to reverse. The names that seemed most popular with fans (and with me) were Red Wolves (a nod to the old name, but with a cool animal attached) or Warthogs (which has alliteration with Washington and could be shortened to 'Hogs to reference the famous Hogs offensive line of the glory days). There is a contingent of fans that actually liked the name Washington Football Team and many would probably still take it over Commanders, but I always suspected it was more driven by nostalgia for the old name and a feeling that if we can't have that name, then no name is better. Washington Football Team feels to me more like having no name and certainly doesn't lend itself to new branding. I'd rather have a new team name and branding, it just needs to be a good name and good branding.

Q: It's the end of 2026 and the beginning of 2027. No changes have been made yet. Dan Quinn is the head coach, Adam Peters is the GM, the roster is intact. If you can make one change to the Commanders team/organization to set them on the right path, what do you do?

A: Unless the rest of the season plays out very differently than it has up until now, I would fire Dan Quinn and let Adam Peters lead a search to choose the next head coach. I think Adam Peters has actually done a pretty good job of rebuilding the roster and giving the team enough depth to withstand an avalanche of injuries this year. However, they often look poorly coached, with the most yards erased by penalty in the NFL, slow playcalls and players taking too much time to get into position, and regular mistakes in situational awareness and game management that lose games.

However, one other change needs to be made. The biggest reason the team was able to go on that 2024 playoff run and has been unable to repeat is that our 2024 season was one of our healthiest ever, with few major injuries to core players in the regular season. That's a major outlier, as Washington has had the most Adjusted Games Lost (AGL) due to injury in the NFL since 2009 (!) and only the Giants have been in the same tier of AGL. This year is no different, with four of the team's highest-paid players already done for the season. To be one of the NFL's most-injured teams over that span of time is significant and unusual in that it covers multiple front office staffs, coaching staffs, and even medical staffs.

The one constant in that time has been the strength and conditioning staff, led by Chad Englehart. Englehart started as an assistant strength and conditioning coach in 2010 before being promoted to head of strength and conditioning in 2017. He's stayed on so long because he's extremely popular with players and rates highly in NFLPA surveys, but I'm convinced his staff are doing something that leads to Washington's players being more injury prone, perhaps by over-training them. An outlier injury rate over 17 years can't be simple bad luck. I would order a full external evaluation of the team's strength & conditioning program and make major changes there.

Q: Who are you happier to see fail this season: The Cowboys or the Eagles?

A: It's a delight to see both of them fail, but more so the Eagles. The Eagles have come to be seen by people around the NFL as the "class of the division" and their fans love to loudly reiterate that belief. It's great seeing them get taken down a peg with a nightmare season most didn't see coming. I've noticed there's a bit of an age gap in how people respond to this question. Most fans over 50ish years of age hate the Cowboys more and still vividly remember "we want Dallas" chants and the heyday of the rivalry from the 80s and 90s, but I think younger fans would generally prefer to watch the Eagles flounder.

Q: What's your happiest memory of the Washington team over the last 30 years? What's been the pinnacle of being a fan of this team since the mid 90s?

A: Honestly, my happiest memory in that time period was when Dan Snyder finally sold the team. His rotten ownership had been the millstone around the team's neck that prevented it from ever rising up and ensured it was always surrounded by negative drama. Most fans by that point knew we'd never be a serious football operation with Dan Snyder in charge, so the sale was the first real light after a long period of darkness that signalled things could finally change.

I wasn't prepared for how quickly that would happen though, because then followed the Commanders 2024 season with a dynamic rookie QB. That season blew out anything that happened under the Dan Snyder era: first time the team won 12 regular-season games since the '91 Super Bowl team, first time the team made the NFC Championship game since the '91 team, etc. In addition, so many of those games ended in exciting, last-minute wins that the team got the nickname "Cardiac Commanders." That season was the pinnacle of being a fan of the team since the mid-90s. The victory over the Lions in the playoffs was the single best game, because nobody expected us to boat race the Lions and advance to the conference championship like that.

#2855. Jayson Tatum admits Charlotte ‘feels like home’ after NBA Cup masterclass

Despite being hundreds of miles away from Boston, Jayson Tatum had no trouble feeling at ease in Charlotte, North Carolina, on Friday night. For a moment, the Spectrum Center even began to sound like TD Garden.

Chants of 'Let's go Celtics' began filling the arena. In response, the Hornets began turning up the volume on their signature buzzing sound effect in an attempt to drown out the Celtics fans taking over Charlotte. It didn't work. When Tatum arrived at the free-throw line in the third quarter, he was greeted by a chorus of loud 'MVP' chants.

"It definitely feels like home," Tatum confessed after Boston's 119-80 NBA Cup win, per CLNS Media.

Tatum found his footing and began painting his latest masterpiece early on. He scored or assisted on 30 of the Celtics' first 40 first-quarter points, which tied Paul Pierce for the most 15-point first quarters (106) in the franchise's play-by-play history, according to ESPN Insights. By halftime, he had reached 24 points on 8-of-14 shooting, including 5-of-8 from beyond the arc, surpassing his combined 3-point makes from his three previous games.

If he wanted to, Tatum could've pursued his career-high (60 points). But instead, his night was called off after three quarters as the Celtics held a 96-57 runaway lead.

At that point, the damage was already done. Tatum only needed three frames to finish with 34 points, eight rebounds, and nine assists, falling a hair shy of securing his first triple-double of the season. He earned a fourth quarter of rest, watching from the bench as head coach Joe Mazzulla allowed reserves including Luka Garza, Mike Conley, and Ron Harper Jr. to get their reps in until the final buzzer.

The Celtics found a way to turn a trip to Charlotte into a home-away-from-home experience. For Tatum, as uplifting as the Boston fans in attendance may have been, the 28-year-old had other reasons to feel comfortable in North Carolina, dating back to his teenage years.

"I have a lot of connections here in this state, this area," he explained. "I came here as an 18-year-old kid, my first time spending real time away from home. I was here for a little under a year, and obviously the connection I have here with Duke and the relationships that I've been able to build. I always love coming back to North Carolina and love playing here. A lot of Celtics fans, a lot of Duke fans. It's always a good time coming back."

Throughout his career, Tatum has always flipped the switch in Charlotte. He's averaged 29.9 points with eight rebounds and 3.7 assists across 15 career games — not including Friday nights — against the Hornets on the road.

CHARLOTTE, NC – NOVEMBER 6: Jayson Tatum #0 of the Boston Celtics shoots the ball during the game against the Charlotte Hornets during the 2026 Emirates NBA Cup on November 6, 2026 at Spectrum Center in Charlotte, North Carolina. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Kent Smith/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images

For as many 'MVP' chants as Tatum has drawn and will continue to draw this season, this performance certainly lived up to the billing. He did everything. He entered the night shooting 41.8 percent from the field and 22.9 percent from three before going 56.3 percent and 62.5 percent, respectively, in Charlotte.

"It was a pretty damn good night," Payton Pritchard told reporters, per CLNS Media. "34 is pretty good."

Tatum unleashed his dominance, both as a scorer and as a playmaker. He was the undisputed leader, carrying out a belt-to-backside thrashing that took Hornets head coach Charles Lee's group out of contention well before the game had reached its end.

He also got to the line plenty, going a perfect 11-for-11 from the charity stripe.

Pritchard continued: "He plays the right way, and he makes great decisions and [he's] one heck of a ball player for sure."

In each of his first eight appearances this season, Tatum has recorded six-plus assists.

It's been only eight months since Tatum returned from his ruptured Achilles tendon last season, which is much more recent than it might sound. He's still working toward completing his first full season since returning, and as much as he's continued to pass the eye test, Tatum still doesn't consider himself 100 percent just yet.

"Hell no," Tatum told CelticsBlog's Noa Dalzell. "I wish. I'm getting there, but no. How I felt before I got hurt was really, really good. I don't feel too far, and again, I still only played less than 40 games since I've been back, so still in the quote-unquote rehab phase of returning to play."

Still, he isn't discouraged by the process.

"We're gonna get there, though," Tatum added.

On Wednesday, the Celtics survived letting go of a 22-point lead against the Milwaukee Bucks as Tatum rested on the sidelines. In Charlotte, they witnessed Tatum make the most of his additional rest and take another step toward becoming the leader Boston will need this season.

#2854. Drew Rosenhaus after Brandon Aiyuk's meeting with 49ers: "To be continued"

It has become abundantly clear that the NFL is delaying the reinstatement of 49ers receiver Brandon Aiyuk from the reserve/left squad list. It has also become abundantly clear that the 49ers hope to squeeze some cash out of Aiyuk before the league lets him back in.

It’s no surprise, then, that Friday’s sit-down between Aiyuk, agent Drew Rosenhaus, and the 49ers did not resolve the situation.

“Hey, guys,” Rosenhaus told a group of reporters who had staked out the Friday meeting. “To be continued. We don’t have any further statements right now. But when we do, we’ll let you know.”

That seems to be precisely where things stand. And the question becomes whether Aiyuk will be willing to strike a deal with the 49ers in order to secure the ability to return to the NFL, with another team.

#2848. Rams listed Matthew Stafford with elbow injury because reporters asked about ice on it

On Monday, reporters asked Rams coach Sean McVay about quarterback Matthew Stafford having ice on his throwing arm after Sunday’s win over the Chargers. On Wednesday, the Rams listed Stafford as having an elbow injury.

“Really, it’s because you guys asked me about it earlier in the week,” McVay told reporters on Friday regarding the decision to disclose an elbow injury for Stafford. “It’s more semantical than anything else. It’s normal, like what he told you guys, but because you guys asked me about him having ice on his elbow. . . . He’s been full, hasn’t missed any sort of reps so normal management stuff that he’s been doing over the last few years.”

It conjures memories of the Patriots’ one-time habit of listing former quarterback Tom Brady as “probable” with a “right shoulder” injury. That all started because he had ice on his shoulder in the locker room, reporters inquired, and the team decided to just put him on the injury report every week.

Has the elbow situation affected Stafford’s throwing?

“I haven’t seen any of that,” McVay said. “I told you guys he’d be better equipped to talk about it. He’s been a full participant, been awesome. He’s spinning the ball. He’s been able to activate all parts of the field with great timing, rhythm, and accuracy so he’s been great.”

So either he has an actual elbow injury that the Rams had been concealing, or he doesn’t really have an elbow injury but they listed him as having one because reporters noticed ice on his arm and asked McVay about it. Neither explanation seems to reflect the true spirit of the injury report, which expects real injuries — and only real injuries — to be disclosed.

Either Stafford has an elbow injury that was previously hidden or he doesn’t have an elbow injury and the claim that he has one is a middle finger to the meddling reporters who were doing their jobs. Neither explanation is a preferred alternative to the unvarnished truth.

#2846. The Protect College Sports Act could be dead

This week’s midterm elections will dramatically reshuffle the deck in Congress. And that could keep those who want the Protect College Sports Act from having the cards necessary to get it passed.

The last, best hope for a Congressional bailout to the college sports system (at the expense of the athletes in the revenue-generating sports) comes in the upcoming six-week lame-duck session. The bill has cleared the Senate. The House of Representatives, which disbanded in the middle of September to block a push for the impeachment of U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, has done nothing with it.

The question now becomes whether the short-timers in the House will muster the will to push their own version of the PSCA through to a successful vote.

Senator Ted Cruz (R-Texas), who co-sponsored the original bill, seems to realize that if it doesn’t happen now it never will.

“There is no realistic path to secure the same broad bipartisan support for a new bill in 2027 and beyond,” a spokesperson for the Senate Committee on Commerce, led by Cruz, told The Athletic. “Passing the Senate-approved bipartisan bill through the House and sending it to the President’s desk during the lame duck Congress gives House Republicans an opportunity to close out the 119th Congress with a significant win for President Trump, HBCUs, women’s sports, and student athletes. An attempt to amend it would be a surefire defeat for the colleges and fans counting on PCSA’s enactment.”

At this point, do House Republicans want to give Trump a win? Right or wrong, those who won’t be coming back in January surely believe they lost their bids for re-election because of him. If so, they’ll feel no compulsion to spend time and effort on another presidential pet project at a time when the list of real issues that need to be addressed keeps growing.

If anything, the House would pass an amended version that would require reconciliation while the clock on the 119th Congress ticks toward midnight. The fact that the Senate Commerce Committee regards even an attempt to amend the existing bill as a “surefire defeat” for the bill will make the current House members who soon will be former House members even more likely to say, “Why bother?”

#2843. Patrick Mahomes is closing in on the record for most TD passes in a QB's first 10 years

Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes is three touchdown passes away from the NFL record for the most ever in a player’s first 10 seasons.

Mahomes, who is in his 10th NFL season, has 325 career touchdown passes, counting the playoffs. Only Peyton Manning, who had 327 touchdown passes in his first 10 years in the league, has had more.

So if Mahomes throws for two touchdowns on Sunday against the Jets, he’ll tie Manning’s record. With three touchdowns, Mahomes will have the record all to himself.

As a rookie, Mahomes played in only one game and didn’t throw any touchdowns. In the eight and a half seasons since then, Mahomes has 279 touchdown passes in the regular season, and another 46 in the playoffs.

Once Mahomes breaks the record, he’s likely to own it for a long time. The only active quarterback who’s closing in is Josh Allen, who is currently in his eighth NFL season and has 260 career touchdown passes. Allen has a chance of throwing for 68 touchdown passes in the next year and a half and moving ahead of Manning, but he’s highly unlikely to finish next season ahead of whatever Mahomes’ total is by the end of this season. This is a record Mahomes will own for a long time.

#2842. Myles Garrett: Rams' opponents will have to pick their poison, me or Aaron Donald

Rams defensive end Myles Garret and defensive tackle Aaron Donald will finally be on the field together Sunday in Washington, and Garrett says that’s going to be bad news for opposing offenses for the rest of the season.

But now Garrett is back, and he said he and Donald playing together can give the Rams an “elite defense” for the rest of the season.

#2841. Winners & Sinners: Week 3

Welcome to Winners & Sinners, where we reflect on the week that was for the Milwaukee Bucks. Week 3 saw the Bucks go 0-3, with the team losing to the Minnesota Timberwolves, Boston Celtics, and Toronto Raptors, despite some valiant efforts that put them in positions to win. But who's deserving of the hardware?

Prior to the Raptors game, this was a legitimate conversation between Myles Turner and Tyler Herro. Then Turner pulled one of his all-too-common vanishing acts. Meanwhile, Herro put in his best playmaking performance as a Buck to make it a no contest. And although he's struggled in first quarters—zero first-quarter points this week—it hasn't really mattered. He heats up. Quickly. But as Nate O. said in our staff thread, "he's definitely more than just a microwave—he's an air fryer."

And so the nickname was born: Tyler Herro, the Air Fryer. Please make this a thing.

The Contenders: Myles Turner, Ryan Rollins.

The Decision: I was so ready to anoint Turner as the defensive champion following his showings against the Timberwolves and Celtics, where he was a force blocking shots, accumulating seven across the two games, and also doing yeoman's work on the boards (at least for him). Then he made it look like the Bucks would have to give up picks in any swap for Jakob Poeltl. Rollins had his moments too, especially when hounding Derrick White. But this belt ain't no participation award; folks need to take it. And so it's still collecting dust in the locker room.

This week's champion is Sausagemahoney, who raised a very thought-provoking question about the Bucks' decision to take Brayden Burries over Yaxel Lendeborg, who's since given the zombie Golden State Warriors new life—and who legend Chris Mullin thinks is "going to be a perennial All-Star and just an All-NBA type":

Truthfully, I'm just jealous I didn't pose the question for this week's Bucks Reacts Survey.

If, prior to the season, someone told you that Nate Ament would play fourth-quarter minutes for the Bucks—not the Herd—in the third week of the season, you'd have assumed it would come in garbage time. If they told you he would be a key contributor in a 22-point comeback, splashing an above-the-break three-pointer to cut the lead to two, you'd have called them crazy. Yeah, the Bucks didn't go on to win this one. And, yes, the Bucks are in the trenches. But moments like this give you a reason to believe.

No hesitation, no rim. No ceiling. Not for this rookie.

Whoever coined "Kuzmania" absolutely nailed it—even if it was originally intended as a positive. Like "mania's" psychiatric denotation, Kyle Kuzma's game is just all over the place far too often for a tenth-year veteran. This week's case in point came at the 2:59 mark of the fourth quarter against the Boston Celtics when, after coming back from a 22-point deficit and down only two, Kuzma decides to take a corner three with 19 seconds left on the shot-clock. 19! It wasn't even as if he was hot—he'd hit only two field goals all game. Of course, after it clanks off rim, the Celtics go on to collect multiple offensive rebounds on the next possession, before Derrick White makes an and-one layup to extend the lead to five. Game over. But the most infuriating thing isn't even that it cost the Bucks the win, it's that Kuzma is supposed to be a veteran presence teaching the Bucks' youth. Some lesson.

If Taylor Jenkins moving Brayden Burries into the starting lineup is a signpost of his willingness to tinker, then he has to do so elsewhere too. There is absolutely no reason to continue to start Kuzma and play him heavy minutes. None!

That's all for Week 3. Share your winners and sinners in the comments!

#2839. After career-low numbers in 2025, Justin Jefferson's production is even lower in 2026

Vikings wide receiver Justin Jefferson had his worst season in 2025. When a great player like Jefferson has an off year, the hope is that he’ll bounce back the next year. That hasn’t happened.

Jefferson’s stats are actually worse across the board in 2026 than they were in 2025, when he seemed to have reached the bottom of what a player his caliber is capable of producing.

Last year, Jefferson finished with a career-low 1,048 receiving yards. This year, heading into Week 9, Jefferson has just 335 receiving yards.

Last year, Jefferson averaged a career-low 12.5 yards per catch. This year, Jefferson is averaging 12.0 yards per catch.

Last year, Jefferson had a career-low 47 receiving first downs. This year, Jefferson has 17 receiving first downs.

Last year, Jefferson averaged a career-low 4.9 catches per game. This year, Jefferson is averaging 4.7 catches per game.

Last year, Jefferson averaged a career-low 61.6 receiving yards per game. This year, Jefferson is averaging 55.8 yards per game.

The major question to ask is whether this means Jefferson has declined, or whether the blame goes to the Vikings’ quarterbacks who haven’t been able to get him the ball over the last two years. An answer to that question may come on Monday night against the Bills, when Carson Wentz starts in place of Kyler Murray, who has been announced as out with a hamstring injury.

Jefferson’s best game this year came in Week 1, when he had just two catches for 11 yards early on with Murray in the game, then caught six passes for 81 yards and two touchdowns from Wentz after Murray left with a concussion. Jefferson also had his best games last year catching passes from Wentz: Jefferson averaged 95.4 yards per game in the five games Wentz started in 2025, and averaged just 47.6 yards per game in the 12 games started by J.J. McCarthy and Max Brosmer.

If Wentz and Jefferson connect for a big game on Monday night, it may spur Vikings coach Kevin O’Connell to decide Wentz is his quarterback going forward. If Wentz can’t get the most out of Jefferson’s playmaking abilities on Monday night, the Vikings may decide on Tuesday morning that it’s time to go shopping for a new quarterback at the trade deadline.

#2837. Report: Colts are in trade talks regarding QB Daniel Jones

The Indianapolis fire sale could indeed extend to the man who was supposed to become a franchise quarterback there.

According to ESPNFL, the Colts have engaged in trade talks this week regarding Daniel Jones, speaking to “multiple teams.”

The precise language of the report identifies only one team as actually talking to the Colts. From the article, the Ravens “were one team to check in on Jones.” The Ravens ultimately struck a deal with the Cardinals for quarterback Jacoby Brissett, whose plunge from No. 1 to No. 3 on the depth chart made it clear to the rest of the league that he was available.

The only other team mentioned by name is the Vikings, and the report points only to "[s]peculation” involving Minnesota. (We’ve been “speculating” about it since the immediate aftermath of Sunday’s loss by the Vikings in Detroit.)

Past ESPNFL reporting on a potential trade for running back Jonathan Taylor ultimately listed five teams as talking to the Colts (Giants, Seahawks, Broncos, Packers, Vikings). The fact that other teams weren’t mentioned as to Jones suggests that, frankly, there may not be other teams.

Really, which current contender would want him? The Vikings are the only potential playoff team that checks the box as possibly needing a starter right now. And only the Vikings and Giants are contenders with which Jones has direct experience. (The Giants wouldn’t want a Jones reunion, and Jones surely wouldn’t want it, either.)

That could change this weekend, obviously. One injury to a starter could alter the dynamics, spurring another contender to pick up the phone and make a push for Jones. The most memorable example of that came 15 years ago, when a broken collarbone to Raiders quarterback Jason Campbell prompted a quick deal for Bengals quarterback Carson Palmer, who had decided he didn’t want to play for the team that had drafted him — and who had yet to report.

Three years ago, Vikings quarterback Kirk Cousins popped an Achilles tendon two days before the deadline, forcing the Vikings to scramble at the deadline to do a deal with the Cardinals for quarterback Josh Dobbs.

Absent a multi-week injury to a starting quarterback on a contender that doesn’t believe its backup can hold down the fort, the Vikings may be the only team that wants Jones at the deadline.

The preferences of Daniel Jones become a factor, too. If (as we firmly believe) he’s not happy that the Colts folded the tents by trading guard Quenton Nelson and defensive tackle DeForest Buckner after a 2-5 start that included an overtime loss to the Chiefs and a toe-to-toe battle with the then-unbeaten Vikings, Jones would have a clear interest in hopping to a contender.

The Vikings wanted to keep Jones after the 2024 season. He opted to sign with the Colts in part because he saw a more realistic path to winning the job over 2023 first-rounder Anthony Richardson in Indianapolis than 2024 first-rounder J.J. McCarthy in Minneapolis. If he’s told that a return to Minnesota would include being installed immediately as QB1, he’d surely prefer that to a lost season with the Colts.

Andd Jones has power over this process. Beyond the basic reality that no team wants a starting quarterback who doesn’t want to play for it, the 2027 roster bonus and base salary that become fully guaranteed in March ($10.51 million) are currently guaranteed for injury. The ESPNFL article mentions that Jones could waive the injury guarantee in order to expedite a deal.

The reverse of that (Jones refusing to waive the injury guarantee) means that Jones could block a trade, if avoiding a potential eight-figure guarantee for 2027 is a dealbreaker for his prospective employer.

Our guess? Right now, only the Vikings currently have interest in Jones. And a trade for Jones becomes a very viable possibility if the Vikings lose to the Bills on Monday with Carson Wentz playing quarterback.

Given the possibility that another team will emerge as a competitor to get Jones, it’s also possible that the Vikings have already decided to trade for Jones after Monday night’s game — win or lose — and that the two teams have agreed to keep it under wraps until Week 9 ends.

Either way, if the oft-injured Jones plays on Sunday against the Cowboys and gets injured, that would kill any chance to trade him. That makes it important to monitor Sunday’s game carefully. If the Colts apply a quick hook to Jones, it could mean that he’s already gone.

He's played over 23 minutes in four out of the last five games and with this being night two of the b2b, we'll see how long Quin Snyder plays him for.

Mikel Brown Jr is not on the injury report, so he'll play tonight and will more than likely sit tomorrow night in Dallas. The Nets are continuing to build Brown Jr and trust that his growth will lead to an exciting future. The drives are there, but if the three pointers start to become consistent, the sky is the limit for him and the Nets. It's all about making the most of the opportunities that are available to you.

Last weekend, the Atlanta Dream fell short in Game 7 of the WNBA Finals against the Golden State Valkyries. The last do-or-die game to decide the W Finals was a pretty celebratory occasion around these parts.

#2834. Ravens reportedly tell Derrick Henry they have "no intention" of trading him

Ravens running back Derrick Henry’s production has plummeted since quarterback Lamar Jackson was first injured before halftime in a Week 4 win over the Titans. And the Ravens have now lost four games in a row.

After Thursday night’s 33-10 loss to the Jaguars, a clearly frustrated Henry (who rarely displays frustration publicly), said he hasn’t mentioned going elsewhere as the trade deadline looms.

Now there’s this, from Adam Schefter of ESPN: “The Ravens recently informed Henry that they have no intention of trading him, according to league sources.”

If “no intention” is used in that assertion in the same way that multiple teams have used “no intention” in the past, a trade remains possible. Because intentions can change.

The Ravens traded for quarterback Jacoby Brissett in an effort to salvage a potential playoff season. Even after Thursday night’s game (which was only the second Jacksonville win in Baltimore since 2000), the Ravens are 4-5 and very much alive for a playoff berth.

In our view, the Ravens would trade Henry only if he made a passionate and compelling case to be traded — and if the Ravens are already considering moving on from the soon-to-be 33-year-old tailback after the 2026 season.

Henry has two former head coaches on current playoff contenders. Former Titans coach Mike Vrabel leads the 5-3 Patriots. Former Ravens coach John Harbaugh runs the 4-2-1 Giants.

The Patriots are without Treveyon Henderson, who will miss his second straight game after developing a sudden and unexplained illness. And the Giants have been linked to Colts running back Jonathan Taylor.

So unless “no intention” means “no way,” it’s still a possibility. At least until 4:00 p.m. ET arrives on Tuesday.

Rams safety Quentin Lake got plenty of attention for comments he made about intercepting a pass thrown by Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert, but on reflection, Lake didn’t like the attention he generated.

#2829. Beating Kyle Shanahan would be quite the feather in Klint Kubiak’s cap

Want to a crystal clear example of the kind of football team Klint Kubiak wants his Las Vegas Raiders to become?

Eye the San Francisco 49ers very closely this Sunday.

Because when Kubiak's Raiders head to Santa Clara to go toe-to-to with Shanahan's Niners, you'll get a bird's eye view a San Francisco team that plays complementary football and is 6-1 overall because of it. There have been fleeting moments of this for Las Vegas, however, the inability to harness consistency is a big reason why the team is 4-4 overall.

Curious as to why Shanahan's football team is one to model for Kubiak?

The pair of head coaches are steeped in the game, thanks to the coaching connection between their fathers Mike Shanahan and Gary Kubiak. The Kyle and Klint dynamic goes back to 1994 when Mike was the offensive coordinator and Gary the quarterbacks coach of the 49ers Super Bowl-winning coaching staff. The elder Shanahan and Kubiak continued to be tied at the hip with the Denver Broncos.

"Not a first one. Just really fortunate to grow up in that environment," Klint Kubiak said on a first memory he had with Kyle Shanahan with their dads coaching together. "I didn't know it at the time, but I got to be exposed to a lot of football at a young age, and I'm very grateful for that, myself and my brothers."

When Gary became the Houston Texans head coach, he gave Kyle his start as an offensive coordinator. And, in 2023, Kyle and Klint joined forces where the Kubiak was the passing game coordinator with the Shanahan dialing up the offense as head coach.

There's mutual respect and trust between the two families. And with a storied history together, similarities were bound to happen.

Foundationally, Shanahan's and Kubiak's respective offenses are deeply rooted in the same coaching tree. It's a philosophy designed to scheme play makers open with pre-snap motions and a balanced attack that showcases a physical and productive ground game. Specializing in the outside/wide-zone run scheme, the 49ers and Raiders eat off play action and the pre-snap motions both play callers habitually use not only identify and stress coverage schemes, but get pass catchers open.

Shanahan and Kubiak know to use running backs and tight ends in a variety of ways, so much so, that pass catching tailbacks and tight ends are often primary targets when the aerial attack is dialed up.

As the longstanding relationship between the two is undeniable, what's also without question is the two having their own distinct twist of the Shanahan-Kubiak offense.

Klint, for example, blended modern, rhythm-based passing concepts into the time-tested zone play-action tenets the system offers.

Taking into account the history between the two and the inherent competitiveness between them, beating Shanahan's 49ers this Sunday would be quite the feather in Kubiak's cap. Even now, there's another branch in the Shanahan-Kubiak dynamic as Klint's brother Klay is the 49ers offensive coordinator.

Like Shanahan, Kubiak won't be alone in his endeavor to coach his team past the 49ers and get his Raiders to back-to-back wins and a 5-4 record instead of a 4-5 mark.

Kubiak's chosen defensive coordinator — Rob Leonard — and special teams coordinator — Joe DeCamillis — must hold up their ends of the bargain in order to play complementary football against a really good 49ers team coming off its bye week. San Francisco is eyeing winning it's seventh game of the year as a proper bounce back from getting beat by the Atlanta Falcons 29-20 two Sunday's ago.

Las Vegas' defense will have its hand full stopping Shanahan and the fact Leonard's group is a cellar dweller statistically league-wise. Playing with much more discipline and urgency, alongside Leonard dialing up blitzes, is a must as the Raiders defense has allowed 30 or more points in the last five games.

"Well, I think if you've worked in the NFL long enough, then that's the reality of our business. It's a production business," Kubiak said of the confidence he has in Leonard. "It's the most competitive industry that I know of, and any time that you start to feel comfortable, then you will be quickly humbled. And so, whether you're having success or you're working to get better, if your mindset stays the same and you continue to push and push through the hard times, you come out on the other end. So, that's the NFL. The NFL brings adversity and makes you answer to it every day."

Offensively, Kubiak has veteran Kirk Cousins at quarterback producing 19 touchdown passes (second most int he league) to just five interceptions. Brock Bowers remains a reliable target for Cousins and is a difficult cover for cornerbacks and safeties, alike.

Cousins speaks highly of the 49ers defense led by Raheem Morris, a defensive coach that left an impression on the Raiders quarterback during their time together with the Washington Commanders.

"It's a great group. They're well coached. Fred Warner is one of the best linebackers in the league. (Nick) Bosa, Buck (DeForest Buckner), several of these guys are some of the best D-linemen in the league, and I think the secondary is also a very good group," Cousins said about Morris' 49ers defense. "They've made a lot of plays, so it's all three levels. You see the safeties really play hard, play fast. They'll strike you.

"So, it's a defense that played really well last year, playing really well this year. I feel like I've seen a lot of these same players and even somewhat the same scheme going back to when Kyle [Shanahan] first got there, and they've got a lot of continuity, and it shows in the tape."

#2827. What's grown at Bayern - and is now making the difference

Beanies pulled over their heads, down jackets already slipped on, Joshua Kimmich high-fived his teammates at the final whistle. The faces of the Bayern players revealed the relief but also the exertion of this afternoon. Once more before the international break, the team gave it everything and got three points. Against opponents who once again asked plenty of questions of FCB.

Our FC Bayern triumphed 2-1 at 1. FSV Mainz 05, maintaining their lead in the Bundesliga standings. It wasn't a victory in which everything happened effortlessly. The hosts defended valiantly, looked for the duels and kept battling until the end. The fact the men from Munich still left as deserved winners is down to, one, the goals from Kimmich and Lennart Karl, and two, how naturally this team now combines technical quality with intensive effort.

"I'd call it a hard-earned victory. For the neutral it certainly wasn't a dazzling display, but still very confident," assessed Kimmich.

Anyone who wanted to understand why Bayern are still unbeaten in the Bundesliga after nine matchdays this season found answers in Mainz. The record champions circulated the ball with precision, moved with purpose and always searched for new passing channels. And if the ball was ever lost, the work to win it back began immediately from the front: with aggressive counter-pressing, short distances and great determination.

That was crucial, particularly against Mainz's compact back five. The hosts made the spaces tight and tried to break up Bayern's rhythm. "Mainz do the dirty things, they always go for the second balls, they're committed in the tackles – that doesn't make it easy. We stood up to that well," commented Aleksandar Pavlović. He and his colleagues accepted the challenge, without losing their style of play.

The numbers back that up: 68.8 percent possession, 717 passes played, of which an impressive 90.9 percent reached a teammate. In addition, 26 attempts on goal and 46 touches in the opposition penalty area. Stats that underline Bayern's dominance, but only tell part of the story.

"We're pleased that we won. We're a little disappointed to have conceded the goal at the end, but we know it's always a tough game here at Mainz. We had to suffer at times, but we were well prepared and stood our ground well," said assistant coach Aaron Danks, who again stood in for head coach Vincent Kompany, who is still recovering from illness.

That the Bavarians were able to convert their superiority into goals is thanks to two special moments. Kimmich put FCB in front with a delightful long-range shot from around 18 metres in the 14th minute, before Karl made it 2-0 in the 57th. Both goals were set up by Harry Kane.

The Ballon d'Or winner once again demonstrated that he's far more than a goalscorer for this team. With eight assists after nine matchdays, Kane has set a new record since detailed data collection began in 2004/05. At the same time, he's already equalled his personal best for one Bundesliga season.

That said, the game also highlighted where Bayern can still improve. Despite 26 attempts, nine shots on target and five big chances, they didn't manage to turn that dominance into a clearer scoreline. That meant Mainz remained in the game, even scored a potential equaliser – which was ruled out for offside – and did bring some renewed tension with a late goal. A reminder that even clear superiority in play is no guarantee for a comfortable win.

And another negative: captain Manuel Neuer was forced off, with Jonas Urbig replacing him between the posts.

The best photos from Bayern's Bundesliga game away at Mainz on Matchday 9 of the 2026/27 season.

When the players went over to their travelling fans after the final whistle, the relief was clear to see. The applause was deserved and the reward for passing a tough test before the forthcoming international break. After that, Bayern return to action against 1. FC Köln at the Allianz Arena (Matchplan).

"What's grown over the last two, three years is very special. There's great calmness at the club. You have the feeling that everything fits. We have to play successful football, that's the basis. But we've seen in the last few weeks that we stick together," summarised Kimmich.

What was Kimmich was describing was also discernible at the MEWA Arena on Saturday. And it's a good foundation for the challenges that lie ahead following the international break.

#2826. What we learned from the Spurs’ win over the Kings

Before the season and even into the first few games, critics have questioned the San Antonio Spurs' four-guard starting lineup. However, through 9 games, that lineup has a +25.4 net rating in 95 minutes and has led the Spurs to a 7-2 start. The bench lineups, especially those without Victor Wembanyama, have caused the team issues. That was never more apparent than in San Antonio's 124-109 thrashing of the Sacramento Kings on Friday night.

Let's be honest about the Kings for a moment. They are a bad basketball team, perhaps not in talent, but in discipline and execution. They lose people on defense and take errant shots on offense. Yet, multiple times on Friday, they gained back ground with most of San Antonio's starters off the floor.

Most of San Antonio's mistakes come from defense, where too often players, especially on the wings, overhelp on a drive or watch the ball, letting the offensive player get an open three or cut to the rim and score over the top of Luke Kornet. San Antonio's defensive lapses were a big reason the Kings shot 49% from the field and hit 46% from three. That second unit's defensive issues don't flip the game against the worst in the league, but against a legitimate, deep team, it could lead to a loss.

The Spurs will take a 15-point win on the road in their first NBA Cup game. But it's hard to come out of that game feeling overly confident about the performance. San Antonio has won seven games in a row, but over half of those have come against teams under .500. A real test awaits them on Saturday in the red-hot Portland Trail Blazers. The Spurs' second unit will need to step up its defensive play if they want to compete with another Western Conference leader.

Devin Vassell is one of the most important players on the Spurs. Vassell is shooting 34.1% from three this season, well below his usual average, which has hurt San Antonio's offense. When he's hitting shots, like he did against Sacramento, the offense opens up a ton for the guards and Wembanyama to dominate the paint. Vassell had 19 points, hitting 5 of his 6 threes on Friday. His off-ball defense was solid, too. He did about all you can ask from a glue guy in the starting lineup. San Antonio will need more performances like these moving forward.

The Kings ran one of the weakest zones I've seen this season, and it led to a big run from the Spurs in the first half. That said, it made me realize that San Antonio is basically built to bust zone defenses. One, Wembanyama is kind of the ultimate cheat code to beat a zone. He can stretch it out on the perimeter or punish smaller players who get caught helping around the basket in the zone. Then, the Spurs have dynamic playmaking guards who are big and physical and can operate in the middle of the zone, a common weak spot in many zone defenses. Add in a couple of knockdown shooters like Vassell and Champagnie, and it becomes nearly impossible to run zone against San Antonio. The Kings tried, and failed to do so on Friday.

Stephon Castle had a rough defensive night, but made up for it with some of the best playmaking we've seen from him this season. He had 19 points, 7 assists, and 1 turnover in the win. One of those assists came on a beautiful inverted pick-and-roll with Wembanyama as the ball handler and Castle as the screener. Castle caught the ball on the short roll, did a 180-degree turn, and fired the ball to a wide-open Vassell for three. It was as close to the Beautiful Game Spurs as San Antonio got on Friday.

Harrison Barnes has earned his spot in the rotation lately, and one could argue he should be getting more minutes than some other bench forward on the roster. He had 13 points on 4-for-7 shooting on Friday against his former team. Offensively, he's a savvy connective player who can take advantage of a defense that is out of position after one of the Spurs' guards creates an advantage. He looks more like the Barnes we saw in his first season with San Antonio, rather than last year. He has essentially replaced Carter Bryant in the rotation, and it doesn't look like he will be giving up that spot any time soon with how he is playing.

I'm interested to see how this team will look once Tobias Harris comes back (hopefully this month?). They desperately need another shot creator and capable defender in that second unit. I know a lot of people want to see him replace Vassell in the starting lineup, but it seems like he could provide even more value as one of the first subs in the game, then playing for a prolonged stretch alongside Kornet and one or two of the guards. The Spurs' top free-agent acquisition should give them more of the versatility many thought the team would have going into the season.

#2823. Cowboys two keys to beating Colts and keeping playoffs hopes alive

The Dallas Cowboys have very possibly not yet defined what "rock bottom" could look like on this 2026 season, but any version of sinking lower than they are right now would involve a second straight loss to a losing team this upcoming Sunday afternoon. The Cowboys are at the Colts, who have not won in over a month.

Many things about this matchup make it feel like it's an opportunity sitting on a tee for Brian Schottenheimer's team to get back in the win column, and just maybe make the run-in to Thanksgiving interesting.

It's time for our weekly look at how the Cowboys can keep alternating wins and losses by bouncing back in week nine, or how they could send this season farther down the drain with another bad loss.

Old friend Daniel Jones at QB for the Colts is the next opponent for the Cowboys to put pressure on, both with their defense (more on that later) and ideally the offense too, by possessing the ball and scoring touchdowns. Jones is 1-8 in his career against the Cowboys, from his past time with the Giants, with four touchdowns and six interceptions in these nine games.

At all three levels of the Colts defense right now, they have problems. Up front, they just traded away DeForest Buckner. At linebacker, Akeem Davis-Gaither will be out on Sunday, with the team already starting rookie C.J. Allen at one of the linebacker positions. In the secondary, former Cowboy Charvarius Ward and Sauce Gardner have not played up to potential and are prone to being beat over the top, and committing costly penalties. Nickel defender Justin Walley is also ruled out against the Cowboys.

The Colts also have the worst turnover differential in the league this season, and have been minus three in two of their last three games, both divisional losses. They do not have a game with a positive margin, and their only neutral game was still a 34-22 loss to Mike McCarthy's Steelers.

With CeeDee Lamb telling the media this week he views the Cowboys offense as beating themselves more than anything, there should be no excuse to not execute the basics against the Colts. Not every drive has to end in points, but not having the focus to stay on the field in short-yardage situations, not getting backed up by unforced penalties, and not finding ways to get the ball to Lamb and George Pickens in space to lean on the Colts all afternoon with this highly-paid offense would be an abject failure.

The Colts defense has not taken the ball away once throughout their active four-game losing streak. If the Cowboys don't turn the ball over and give the Colts extra life and short fields to keep the game close, the talent differential in this matchup should reveal itself and allow the Cowboys to get out of Indy with a win.

Colts star running back Jonathan Taylor might be the obvious choice as the potential game-wrecker against the Cowboys defense in this matchup, especially considering the Colts main objective may actually be getting Taylor's trade value up with a big game against a Dallas defense torched by Tyler Allgeier last week.

Allgeier was certainly a big factor in how the Cardinals made their comeback in Arlington last Sunday, but when the game clearly came down to Gardner Minshew needing to make a throw, he did so as well for the real backbreaking plays against Christian Parker's defense.

The Cowboys also sacked Jacoby Brissett four times last week, but only got to Minshew once with Quinnen Williams doing so in overtime. Daniel Jones was sacked three times last Sunday against the Jags. He was sacked four times against a Vikings defense that blitzed him at a relentless rate that literally broke records for how often a defense could blitz. The week before that, he was sacked six times against the Titans. The Steelers defense only got to Jones once, but still swung the game in their favor by forcing Jones to drop back 44 times compared to 24 total rushing attempts for the Colts in week five.

In Jones' last four starts against the Cowboys, all losses, he's been sacked 16 times. Narrow this down to the last two games, and the Cowboys have won by a combined score of 60-15 with eight sacks, and also three interceptions.

Whether it's with the blitz or trusting Williams, Rashan Gary, and Donovan Ezeiruaku up front, Parker's defense needs to make pressure the priority against this Colts offense. The coverage is not good enough to hold up for long enough periods of time to be trusted more than the Cowboys should trust their ability to get to Jones before he can even throw the ball, and the same goes for run defense. Sacks to get the Colts behind the chains is what this defense should be after more than anything.

#2821. Luka Doncic's historic run jump-starts early MVP conversation

Ten games is too early for most valuable player conversation. Just don't tell fans at Crypto.com Arena.

"M-V-P! M-V-P!" the Lakers faithful chant at Luka Doncic every time the Lakers guard toes the free-throw line.

After dropping a season-high 53 points during the Lakers' 124-118 win over the Portland Trail Blazers on Friday, Doncic is averaging 40.1 points, 7.8 rebounds and 7.7 assists in a scoring binge for the ages. He's the fourth Laker to have four consecutive games of 40 or more points. He's the third to have seven games of 35 or more points.

And he's doing it efficiently: Doncic's sky-high shooting percentage dipped to 49.8% after an unusually cold 5-for-15 shooting night from three-point range Friday. He was still 12 for 18 from two-point range.

Here are three takeaways from Friday's win:

Lakers guard Luka Doncic shouts after sinking a three-pointer that gave the Lakers a five-point lead over Portland in the third quarter Friday at Crypto.com Arena. (Gina Ferazzi / Los Angeles Times)

Walker Kessler just shook his head as he grasped for the right words. There might not be many more left to describe what Doncic is doing.

"He's my MVP," the Lakers center said eventually.

Being in the most valuable player conversation isn't new for Doncic. The two-time scoring champion finished third in MVP voting in 2024 with Dallas. He averaged 33.9 points, 9.2 rebounds and 9.8 assists during the regular season, then led the Mavericks to the NBA Finals.

Each season the do-it-all guard is among the favorites to win the award. But Doncic's early-season campaign feels different. Not only is Doncic in great shape, Portland coach Micah Nori said before Friday's game, but Doncic also has the right pieces around him after the Lakers remade their roster to complement the star with floor-spacing shooters, strong perimeter defenders and a rolling center.

"It's a perfect offensive storm," Nori said. "He's the MVP right now. Hands down."

Lakers coach JJ Redick does not engage in MVP discussion until 50 games in, he said. When told Doncic topped NBA.com's first MVP ladder Friday, the Lakers coach brushed aside any chance to make a grand proclamation.

In the premature MVP rankings, Doncic was ahead of San Antonio Spurs center Victor Wembanyama. The 22-year-old is averaging 29.1 points, 12.6 rebounds, three assists and 4.2 blocks per game.

Doncic's 53-point outburst eclipsed Wembanyama's 52 points the star center scored Wednesday for the highest single-game scoring performance this season. But Wembanyama also grabbed 24 rebounds with eight blocks in a historic statline matched only by Wilt Chamberlain.

The French superstar finished second in MVP voting last year and was the first unanimous defensive player of the year in league history. His outsized defensive impact was a significant part of why he entered the season as the betting favorite to win his first MVP.

Read more: Swanson: Luka Doncic can lead Lakers to a title, but only if his teammates pull their weight

Doncic, who didn't get any votes from NBA general managers when asked in a preseason survey who they thought would win the MVP, said he's determined to step up on defense for his team. He is averaging 1.7 steals per game, which ranks second among Lakers players. His four drawn charges is tied for most in the league.

"He has a pride and he has a hunger," Lakers forward Sandro Mamukelashvili said of Doncic's defense. "He has a will to not be labeled as that guy who you can just attack."

Doncic is challenging Chamberlain's stats on the offensive end. His 361 points through his first nine games are the most for a player since Chamberlain's 472 points in 1962-63. No one has averaged 40 points over a season since the legendary center in 1963. The possibility has barely crossed Doncic's mind.

"As long as we win, I'm good," Doncic said.

The Lakers are 8-2 with the best record in the Western Conference. They have not started 8-2 since their last championship season.

Lakers forward Adou Thiero drives to the basket between Portland's Scoot Henderson (00) and Jrue Holiday (5) at Crypto.com Arena on Friday. (Gina Ferazzi / Los Angeles Times)

Adou Thiero had a loud four points, four rebounds and two assists in his long-awaited season debut Friday. The energetic forward missed the first nine games of the season because of swelling in his left knee. He didn't waste any time reintroducing himself to the team, keeping a loose ball alive on his first offensive possession that led to an offensive rebound and a put-back from Mamukelashvili.

"He literally did everything we asked him to do," Redick said.

The second-year forward has been hampered by his balky left knee since college, when he missed the end of his junior season after surgery. The procedure delayed the beginning of his rookie season and when he returned, a sprained MCL in his right knee knocked him out for six more weeks.

The injuries prevented Thiero from gaining any traction. This summer, when he had the longest stretch of sustained health during his short professional career, he could finally show teammates and coaches what he could do.

Thiero jumped out of the gym during practices. He smothered teammates while guarding the ball. He brought the same energy to the court Friday when it counted.

"We value Adou a lot," Kessler said. "He's a very physical player, really talented, athletic player."

Lakers forwards Ziaire Williams, left, and Sandro Mamukelashvili double team Portland guard Sidy Cissoko as he attempts a layup at Crypto.com Arena on Friday. (Gina Ferazzi / Los Angeles Times)

The Lakers missed their first 15 three-point shots. It felt like a minor miracle they trailed by only seven at halftime.

The most dynamic offense in the league had to rely on its defense. The Lakers forced 24 turnovers and held the Trail Blazers (6-2) to 15 points in the third quarter.

"It's nice to know when you're not making shots that you can also rely on your defense to help keep you in the game," said forward Jake LaRavia, who had seven points, eight rebounds and one steal.

The Lakers rank 21st in defensive rating, giving up 113.6 points per 100 possessions. They are one of the worst rebounding teams in the league, ranking 29th despite outrebounding the Trail Blazers by three. Their defense instead relies on blocks and steals.

The Lakers are tied for third in the NBA with 10.7 steals per game. Matisse Thybulle leads the team with 1.8 steals per game. Austin Reaves had a team-high four steals Friday.

#2820. Max Verstappen watched Premier League football during Brazilian GP qualifying delay: "12 hours I'll never get back"

Max Verstappen called it a day after Q1 during Formula 1 qualifying in Sao Paulo, as he already knew he would be starting from the back of the grid for the Brazilian Grand Prix due to an engine-related grid penalty.

In the FIA's 'indicative grid', Verstappen is listed in 21st place, behind Lewis Hamilton and just ahead of Sergio Perez.

The four-time world champion once again demonstrated in Q1 just how competitive he can be in wet conditions. His first flying lap was 1.4 seconds faster than the time at the top of the leaderboard at that point, and four tenths quicker than Hamilton, who crossed the start-finish line shortly afterwards. The Red Bull driver eventually finished the opening segment of qualifying in third place – behind Lando Norris and George Russell – before climbing out of the car.

Lewis Hamilton, Charles Leclerc and Max Verstappen hit with F1 grid penalties for Brazilian GP

Asked whether he had at least enjoyed himself to some extent in the Brazilian rain, Verstappen replied in the media pen: "Not really, because I'm not fighting for anything. My mind is already set on tomorrow, so it was just about doing a lap, not risking anything. Every lap that I did, we were up there, but for me that's not a surprise."

Like his fellow drivers, Verstappen had to wait almost an hour and a half because of the red-flag delay before he could even get out on track. Asked how he had spent that time during the heavy rainfall, Verstappen laughed in front of Viaplay's camera: "Watching football. Premier League."

Asked which match he had been watching exactly, Verstappen continued: "A lot of different games, but Nottingham Forest-Manchester City was the last one before I got into the car. It was 3-1, I actually saw a great goal just before I got back in!"

When it was pointed out that fans might find it hard to believe Verstappen had been watching football shortly before having to tackle qualifying in extremely difficult conditions, the Dutchman responded calmly: "But I'm starting last anyway, so it doesn't matter. I've lost 12 hours of my life today that I'll never get back."

While there was nothing at stake for Verstappen on Saturday, Sunday will naturally be a different matter. Verstappen has already produced three memorable comeback races at Interlagos, including in the past two seasons.

In 2024, Verstappen won from 17th on the grid, effectively nipping Norris's remaining title ambitions in the bud, while last year the Dutchman drove from the pitlane to the podium.

Starting from the back row therefore does not necessarily mean he has no chance, but Verstappen believes fighting his way through the field with the 2026 cars will be considerably more difficult.

"It was [possible to fight back] in the past, but now we don't have DRS anymore. And the overtake mode is very limiting around here, because of the long straight," Verstappen said.

"Everyone is draining the battery, so your speed difference on the straight is going to be a lot less. It will be a bit like Mexico really, so it will be quite a lot harder to pass than normal."

Nevertheless, rain could of course lend a helping hand. Rain is once again forecast for tomorrow in Sao Paulo, which was also one of the considerations behind Ferrari's decision to take grid penalties for both drivers here.

#2816. Oso Ighodaro is starting; is that a good thing?

The Phoenix Suns moved Oso Ighodaro into the starting lineup for Thursday's win against the Orlando Magic. Many called for a change to the lineup (or multiple changes, which is another article for another day). He is a somewhat polarizing player, with staunch fans and outspoken skeptics. I'll make a case for this being absolutely the right move for this team, right now.

Khaman Maluach is learning game by game. Working on his body (and hopefully hands) to get stronger. He has an awesome frame and, at 20 years old, is just beginning to learn the nuances of NBA success. He has a mostly high effort level and wants to be good. However, the NBA is littered with players thrust into action before developing properly – and then losing confidence, picking up bad habits. Time on the court in meaningful minutes is needed to progress toward the objective of becoming a solid NBA starting center. The current situation with Mark Williams out well into 2027 allows for consistent 15-20 minute nights. Handing the "starter" keys could put him on a path more closely aligned to former Suns top-10 pick Josh Jackson (sorry to those with draft PTSD here).

Back to Oso. The Phoenix starting lineup needs more connectivity and flow on offense? Check. Struggling horrifically on defense? Check. Per HoopsJunkie.io, Ighodaro's on/off defensive rating of -17.2 points per 100 possessions ranks EIGHTH in the NBA! This is in spite of being a below-average defensive rebounder (141st in the NBA in DREB%). Keep in mind, he suffered a right oblique strain in the opener and is likely just rounding back into form now. I've referenced DARKO several times as a great tool to project overall player value at a moment in time.

Through last season, his projected value was steadily growing. Once fully healthy, it is reasonable to expect that progression to continue. He looks bigger and stronger. His turnovers are down. While the results are not there yet at the free-throw line, he looks smoother (and commentators have noticed the same). With a DARKO of 1.0, compared to a -1.6 for Maluach, the model predicts more positive impact on winning in the present.

Oso and Ryan Dunn, to an even greater extent early this season, are developing players. They show what development can look like for players drafted 40th and 28th, respectively. With his raw talents (drafted 10th) and willingness to work, Maluach's ultimate success depends on development done the right way. This franchise needs Man Man to get there for the long run – and needs Oso right now to stabilize a starting lineup that was in disarray.

#2811. Stats Rundown: 5 numbers from the Mavericks 112-100 Emirates Cup win over the Jazz

The Dallas Mavericks were in a funk for their past two games, with Kyrie Irving sitting one and Cooper Flagg having arguably the worst two-game stretch of his young career. Emirates Cup action raised the intensity and the Mavs stepped up to the tune of a 112-100 win Friday night.

For what felt like the first time in a long time, the Mavs dominated on the boards to the tune of +18 for the night. Dallas knew this was something they needed to work on and they answered the call Friday night. The cherry on top was that rookie Morez Johnson, Jr. led all players 17 boards!

All of those rebounds led to plenty of points for Dallas. They made the most of ending Utah possessions and extending their own possessions, outscoring the Jazz by 15 in second chance points.

The Mavericks got themselves to the line early and often, allowing them to keep the game tight in the first half. Utah was more efficient from the line, missing only a single attempt, but Dallas' 80.6% (25-of-31) was more than enough of an edge, giving the Mavs a +12 advantage from the charity stripe.

The game had an inordinate number of traveling calls; nine to be exact. In the flow of the game, it was quite noticeable and somewhat bizarre. The travel-happy referees were equal opportunity penalizers, handing Utah five of the infractions, and Dallas four of their own.

Dallas opened up a tight game in the third quarter and early part of the fourth. Reeling off a 28-6 scoring run, Dallas extended a one possession game to a 20-point lead. Utah responded with a couple of three-point makes and a smaller run of their own, but that 28-6 run proved to be the deciding factor in a Mavericks' win.

The Mavs needed a win to wash away a bit of the stink from the prior two games and they did all the little things to make it happen against the Jazz. Dallas was locked in on the boards, got to the line, and put together a nice run to build a cushion that proved insurmountable for the Jazz.

#2809. Connor Zilisch Addresses Rumors of Early Hendrick Motorsports Move

Connor Zilisch isn't hiding his interest in driving for Hendrick Motorsports. He just isn't planning to get there ahead of schedule.

The 20-year-old NASCAR driver addressed growing speculation about his future Friday at Homestead-Miami Speedway, where he confirmed that he intends to remain with Trackhouse Racing through the 2027 season before making his anticipated move to Hendrick in 2028.

And while Zilisch acknowledged that an earlier opportunity would be appealing, he offered a compelling reason for staying put: He doesn't believe he's finished learning at Trackhouse.

Zilisch's future has become a popular topic in the NASCAR garage since plans emerged for him to join Hendrick Motorsports in 2028.

The biggest question has been whether that timeline could change, particularly with Alex Bowman's future in the No. 48 Chevrolet drawing attention.

During Friday's media availability, Zilisch was asked directly whether there had been discussions about moving to Hendrick or a Hendrick-affiliated team as early as 2027.

"Yeah, it's been a lot of noise," Zilisch said. "Alex [Bowman] has a commitment to run one more year. I have sponsors to fulfill obligations for another season. I'm excited about that."

He acknowledged that joining Hendrick sooner would be an attractive opportunity, but suggested that remaining at Trackhouse could ultimately serve him better.

"I think it'd be great to go race for Hendrick Motorsports next year and get that opportunity quicker, but at the same time, I'm happy in the spot I'm in," Zilisch said.

His explanation went beyond contractual obligations.

Zilisch believes another season with Trackhouse will allow him to continue developing without the additional scrutiny that comes with driving for one of NASCAR's most successful organizations.

"I get to learn in a lower-pressure situation with less eyeballs on me," he explained. "I feel like I can just go out and focus on myself."

It's a notable admission from a driver whose rapid rise through NASCAR has already brought considerable attention and expectations.

For Zilisch, the decision isn't simply about waiting for an opening at Hendrick. It's also about how he wants to leave Trackhouse.

His rookie Cup Series campaign hasn't delivered everything he hoped, and he made clear that walking away after a disappointing season isn't how he wants to end his time with the organization.

"I would not want to leave Trackhouse after a season like this," Zilisch said. "I want to end on a good note."

That perspective adds another dimension to the speculation surrounding his future.

Rather than treating 2027 as a season to get through before joining Hendrick, Zilisch sees it as an opportunity to build on his rookie experience and help Trackhouse make meaningful progress.

He also recognizes that moving to Hendrick would bring a different kind of pressure, with heightened expectations every weekend.

For now, he believes there's value in having another year to prepare for that responsibility.

"Hopefully next year can go better; we can take something away from it and have a good last season together," Zilisch said.

The destination may already be decided, but Zilisch isn't interested in rushing the journey.

And for anyone expecting an early move to Hendrick Motorsports, his message from Homestead was clear: He still has unfinished business at Trackhouse.

#2807. Falcons vs. Bengals series history: Win-loss record, matchup results

The Falcons head back into play against the AFC this week, and they do so across the pond in the second ever NFL game to be played in the Spanish capital of Madrid, at the esteemed Estadio de Santiago Bernebéu. Their opponent in that game will be the Cincinnati Bengals, who have won two games out of every three against the Birds, owning a very aesthetically pleasing 10-5 all time record against Atlanta.

The majority of that damage came before the turn of the millennia, with the Bengals winning seven out of 10 matchups against the overmatched Falcons through the 1996 season, with games between these teams happening on averaged every three years in that time period.

The Birds pulled back a little bit with three consecutive victories — in 2002, 2006 and 2010 — to pull the series close to even. That was quickly followed with three straight Bengals victories which brings us to where we are today, with two of those coming in the Matt Ryan era, which was also the most successful one in Falcons history. The Bengals caught Atlanta in a down year of that era twice in a row, in 2014 and 2018.

The Falcons had some confidence about them in year 2 of the Arthur Smith regime, having just pulled back to .500 at 3-3, with a victory against the 49ers after some questionable reffing cost them against Tampa the week before. The Bengals sported the same record, but they proved from the start that they were on another level.

It took exactly two minutes for second year man Joe Burrow to hit Tyler Boyd on a 60-yard touchdown to open the scoring. Then after a Falcon punt, the Bengals punched the ball in again following a longer drive. Then an Atlanta three and out was followed with a Burrow to rookie Ja'Marr Chase touchdown on the first play of the second quarter, before the two connected in the end zone again on the back end of the same quarter.

By halftime the game was effectively over as the Falcon offense spent the second half completely one dimensional and getting terrorized by the Bengal defense, with Burrow putting the finishing touches on with a rushing score to complete his magnificent day.

Up 35-17, one of the most impressive feats by the Bengal offense was getting the ball back via punt at their own 3-yard-line (why the Falcons punted it near midfield down three scores in the fourth quarter I don't know) with 8:44 left in the game and choking away that entire clock (and all three Atlanta timeouts) with a 17-play drive which went 95 yards and ended in a kneel down.

#2806. Luka Doncic is soaring, Lakers are No. 1 in West. His brilliance is leaving mark

He had recently likened Luka Dončić to a supernova. He said you have to pick your poison against him.

So, when asked if he had any superlatives to offer following Dončić's 53-point, five-rebound, five-assist performance in the Lakers' 124-118 win over the Trail Blazers on Friday, Redick stumbled.

When a reporter started asking another question, he interjected.

"I'm going to just sit around, we'll gather one day and come up with more superlatives," Redick added. "So I'll have more words ready. But for now, I don't have any words."

The hyper-prepared Lakers coach was finally ill-prepared for an assignment.

Redick isn't the only person who has been left dumbfounded following Dončić's blazing start to the season in which he's averaging a league-leading 40.1 points, 7.7 rebounds and 7.6 assists.

In Friday's game, Dončić passed Michael Jordan (347) for the most points scored in the firstnine games of a season since the NBA-ABA merger with 361 points.

Los Angeles Lakers guard Luka Doncic shoots a free throw during an NBA basketball game against the Portland Trail Blazers in Los Angeles, Friday, Nov. 6, 2026. AP Photo/Mark J. Terrill

It's the most points anyone has scored in the modern NBA since Wilt Chamberlain in 1962-63.

"I'm having a lot of fun," Dončić said. "Obviously playing basketball, it's a lot of fun for me. It's more [fun] when you play like this and when you win games. So, it's been like this my whole life. Basketball was my dream. Playing in the NBA was my dream. Just living my dream."

The 27-year-old face of their franchise is having an MVP-caliber campaign while leading the Lakers to the No. 1 seed in the Western Conference with an 8-2 record.

No one expected the Lakers to be this good.

And no one expected Dončić to soar to the top of the MVP conversation after he hadn't finished in the top two in voting ever in his career.

Los Angeles Lakers guard Luka Doncic, left, drives to the basket against Portland Trail Blazers center Robert Williams III on Friday, Nov. 6, 2026, in Los Angeles. AP Photo/Mark J. Terrill

But if the first few weeks of the season have made anything clear, it's that Redick needs to beef up his vocabulary. He needs to get a thesaurus. Dončić is skyrocketing, and he's carrying the Lakers with him.

There were many incredible moments in the Lakers' 16-point come-from-behind win over the Trail Blazers in which they stormed back after shooting 4-for-23 from beyond the arc in the first half, including missing all 15 of their initial attempts from that distance.

There was the buzzer-beating 62-foot shot that Dončić made at the end of the second quarter, a shot he literally banked in from three-quarters of the court.

"Luka can do some things that maybe a handful, if not no one, can do in basketball," Redick said.

Los Angeles Lakers guard Luka Doncic, left, shoots over Portland Trail Blazers center Robert Williams III on Friday, Nov. 6, 2026, in Los Angeles. AP Photo/Mark J. Terrill

There was a little mixup after Dončić notched his 11th 50-point performance in his career, surpassing Kareem Abdul-Jabbar for 10th-most such games in NBA history.

It all started because Ziaire Williams couldn't wait to congratulate Dončić.

So much so that Williams decided to interrupt what he thought was Dončić's walk-off television interview with "NBA on Prime" by approaching him from behind, putting his hands on his shoulders and yelling, "Fifty ball."

Austin Reaves was doing the interview. Not Dončić.

"I'm the wrong white person," said Reaves, who had 25 points.

Did Williams seriously confuse his two teammates? "Deadass," he said, flashing a smile in the Lakers' locker room.

"That was very disrespectful to me," Dončić said jokingly of being confused with Reaves, with whom he shares a brotherly bond.

It has been a wild stretch for Dončić, who's shattering records nightly.

He's leaving his coach at a loss for words. He's making shots from outer space. And he's leaving his teammates seeing his face in everyone.

"I feel like that," he said. "But as long as we win, I'm good."

#2805. Vikings WR Jauan Jennings declined 49ers interest because "I love where I'm at"

Wide receiver Jauan Jennings has not played a major role in the Vikings offense through the first eight weeks of the season, but he wasn’t interested in switching teams when the possibility presented itself last month.

The 49ers and Vikings discussed a trade that would send Jennings back to the team he played for during his first five NFL seasons and talks progressed to the point that Jennings spoke to his former coach Kyle Shanahan about a return. Jennings expressed a desire to stay with the Vikings and gave a succinct reason for his decision when asked about it on Saturday,

Jennings won’t be improving on his production Monday night as the Vikings ruled him out with a calf injury. That could open the door for Odell Beckham Jr. to make his Vikings debut.
