#2804. Press Taylor explains the importance of Bears RB D'Andre Swift

There were a lot of things that went right for the Chicago Bears in their win against the Seattle Seahawks, including running back D'Andre Swift getting three rushing touchdowns.

Swift currently has 10 rushing touchdowns, the most in the NFL through eight weeks. He has been the most reliable person on Chicago's roster, playing on 62 percent of the Bears' offensive snaps. Especially with Kyle Monangai out the past four weeks, Swift has been a key part of the Bears' offense. Bears offensive coordinator Press Taylor praised Swift for being a dependable player on offense.

"He's reliable," Taylor said. "I mean, he's somebody that we trust a lot in. We want to do our best to keep him as fresh as possible throughout the course of the season. There's certain times where it looks like he could use a breather at times and we're ready to roll with the other guys that need to be available for him right here. Then there's certain times where he feels fresh, he looks fresh, he's ready to go."

Swift didn't have his best rushing performance against the Seattle Seahawks, totaling 27 carries for 69 yards, averaging 2.6 yards per carry (his lowest of the season). But Swift found plenty of success in the red zone with his three rushing touchdowns, tying his season-high.

"I think the other night you saw the production down in the red zone particularly," Taylor said. "It was a tough sled in the run game. We understood that's what it would be really on normal down situations. We wanted to stick with it. We wanted to be able to utilize it at certain times. We wanted to stay on schedule with it. But then in the red zone, I thought those guys did a good job of making things really go, and Swifty was a big part of that. He bounced a couple runs that probably were not intended for the ball to go, and he's able to get the edge and punch it in, which was critical for us. But he's a guy we count on, we trust, and he's produced for us."

Chicago will need Swift to step up once again when they take on the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, who have one of the best run defenses in the NFL and held the Atlanta Falcons scoreless in their last game.

#2802. Den Questions: Finding Identity In Turmoil

Welcome back to the Den. The Wolves are ten games in and their record stands at 7-3. Over that time the Wolves sprinted out of the gates, lost Anthony Edwards to dirty knees in need of a cleaning, and have mostly righted the ship. Their losses are on travel back-to-backs and their first game without Edwards where they didn't even have a chance to practice before tip-off.

This team found something special in their first four games and then had their literal knees cut from them. Through the mire of the early season, as the rest of the league reels from their own injuries, the Wolves are looking for another new identity. An identity that does not include Edwards but prepares for his return.

As you can imagine, there are a lot of questions for this team to answer. Here are some of them.

Note: So much of this is small sample size theater.

It's just flashes. He had similar highs in Golden State before cooling down. There's no way he can keep this up. Here he goes again driving into traffic to get blocked… huh, nice pass. No no no, don't shoot tha…SPLASH! Oh my gawd, he got up so high for that rebound.

This short-staged drama has occurred inside my head in nearly every game this year. In good games and bad, Jonathan Kuminga has shown up to do whatever is asked of him.

In every counting stat except points per game, Kuminga is averaging career bests; rebounds (5.7), assists (2.9), steals (1.2) and blocks (1.0). His highest BPM through his first five seasons was 0.1. This season he is at 2.9 and has his career first positive for Offensive Box Plus Minus (0.6).

Head Coach Chris Finch has heaped praise on JK. In Minnesota's more read and react, flow, style, the Wolves starting power forward is emboldened to make a play when the ball finds him. His cuts aren't always rewarded but it sends the defense into a panic and opens things up for his teammates. It also puts him in the middle of the floor to grab or poke out offensive rebounds.

I am running out of excuses for why it won't last. After the first few games, I thought his play would disappear once the initial novelty of the season's start wore off. It didn't.

I thought he'd become more shot hungry and ball dominant when Ant went down. He hasn't.

I thought he'd get worn down having to guard some of the best players in the league night after night. This might happen as the overlong season grinds on, but so far Kuminga seems to get up for the battle.

The hardest question might be coming, "Can the Wolves afford to keep Kuminga?"

The start of the season has seen a dramatic drop in Rudy Gobert's points per game and his near league-best shooting efficiency. Gobert is averaging his fourth fewest shot attempts, second least points per game, the worst shooting percentage, and worst free throw percentage of his career.

It took one of the smartest basketball minds in Mike Conley over a year to learn how to play with Rudy. LaMelo Ball has had a scant few weeks to build chemistry. Combine that with the geometry of the floor and the defensive attention he is getting due to the sidelined Edwards, and it's no surprise the lack of consistency.

The Wolves need Rudy to be effective on offense. The book is out on the big man. Good defenses know how to bait Minnesota into thinking Rudy is open and recover quick enough to force a turnover or an errant shot.

Which brings us to the question of how to effectively use Gobert on offense. There is space to use him in the pick n' roll, but that has rarely been Finch's play style of choice. He is averaging a career high in offensive rebounds and this is primarily where I want him to find his points.

Finishing those misses just as they bounce off or tipping them out to teammates to try again when defenders are too close to him. Don't give them a chance to send him to the line.

He is very good at screening his teammates open and should continue to be used as the effective body in the way. This opens up Ball, Ayo Dosunmu, and Bones Hyland to get a screen assist into open triples. But this also pulls Rudy away from the hoop and the offensive boards that are his best offense.

Simple as it sounds his threat to roll is only as effective as his chemistry with his point guard. Until that firms up, he's on cleanup duty.

The Wolves are getting spooky with a lot more ghost screens this season. This gambit, that asks a shooting threat to feint a screen before sprinting to the other side of the point-of-attack (POA) defender, is meant to short circuit a defense. In a fraction of a second, the ghost screener's defender has to determine if they need to call for a switch if the screen gets set, or to chase after the shooter who has suddenly burst to a preferred place to spot up.

The Wolves are loaded with players who can quickly turn on the jets (I can't recommend Ayo Dosumnu's Player's Tribune piece enough) and make this decision that much harder. Screens are overcome best when a defense is communicating. The threat of a ghost screen shortens that window for effective communication.

If the POA defender thinks a screen is about to be set, they might get ready to hedge for the incoming contact giving the ball handler enough wiggle room to drive. If the chase defender thinks a screen is being set, they might slow up enough to give the ghost screener a chance to find an open look. If a screen is set, the game flows into common pick n' roll, one of the most tried and true means of creating advantages.

In the clip below, the Wolves use a combination of screens to break Orlando's zone, a past bugaboo for Minnesota.

Armed with better outside shooting than the past two years, look for the Wolves to continue to haunt perimeter defenders with these scary non-screens.

Note: Every injury to a player is unique. No timeline to return or level of ability when returning is the same. An Achilles tear for Donte DiVincenzo and his play style is a completely different injury that an Achilles tear for Ariel Hukporti and how he approaches the game, despite hurting the same tendon.

The day after it was announced that Ant would get arthroscopic knee surgery, a friend of mine sent me a grim text. All he could think of was Grant Hill, Brandon Roy, and Penny Hardaway and the possibility that Ant's career would be sapped from him like it had from those elite athletes.

I immediately texted back "What about DWade, Kobe, CP3?" After a brief internet search here are several NBA players who have undergone arthroscopic knee surgery who had some of their best years after the fact.

Kobe Bryant – Kobe had his first knee surgery in 2003, another in 2006, and another in 2010. In the midst of this string of surgeries he was an All-Star every year (despite the Laker bump, these were earned), won an MVP and was top five in MVP voting in all but one year, and made All-Defensive Teams in every year but one.

Dwyane Wade – DWade (a frequent Ant comp) had his entire left meniscus removed in 2002 while in college and went on to have a Hall of Fame career where he was unwillingly nicknamed Flash for how quick he was despite playing sans knee cartilage.

Chris Paul – Snitch Paul had arthroscopic knee surgery to repair a meniscus tear in 2010 while still with the New Orleans Hornets. As fun as he was on those Hornets teams, the Point God emerged into a force in the years after with the Lob City Clippers, Hardenball Rockets, and even made his first Finals with the Phoenix Suns, 11 years after the surgery.

Jimmy Butler – General Soreness had surgery on his right knee in 2018 while the Wolves were third in the Western Conference. He returned to help break the 14 year playoff drought. Jimmy has since been the driving force to two NBA finalist teams, never winning one. He adds multiple All-Star selection, an All-NBA selection, and an All-Defensive Team honor to his otherwise championship barren trophy case. I'm not bitter.

Jaylen Brown – Mr. Lamb Chops and Gravy had a knee procedure in the summer of 2025 and was back by training camp en route to being an All-Star, All-NBA 2nd Team, and sixth in MVP voting.

This surgery to clean up Ant's knee will likely diminish Ant's burst athleticism. He has moved his game to more outside shooting while maintaining a rim presence. If his downhill game is not as quick, it will hurt, but he's also added a midrange for if the defender goes too far under that leaves him a three level problem for any defense.

Plenty of NBA greats have bounced back, here's hoping Ant joins this laudable list.

Ant is out for roughly two months. Terrance Shannon Jr. has missed two games with a hip contusion. Donte DiVincenzo is recovering from an Achilles tear with every intention of coming back this season.

In their absence the Wolves have slotted Ayo Dosunmu into the starting lineup. Bones Hyland is scoring the ball well. Jaylen Clark is getting into guys jerseys and hitting 41.2% of his threes on 2.1 attempts a game.

All of these players are competing with each other for minutes. While the deeper bench has done yeomen's work to keep the Wolves head above water, they are not as good as the players whose minutes they are sopping up.

Finch is strict in his rotations. In the last three years, his starting lineups are in the top five for most used lineups in the NBA. If he gets a fully healthy team, Bones and Clark's minutes will likely disappear all together. Ayo will move back into his sixth man role ready to be whatever his team needs of him.

Donte is the biggest question mark. He started all 82 games last season, but there is not a spot for him in this starting lineup. We also don't know what he will look like coming back from such a devastating injury.

Sans LaMelo foul trouble giving Bones more minutes in the Raptors game, Finch has only given double digit minutes out to nine players before the injuries started. Joan Beringer's minutes aren't going anywhere. Trey Lyles has size, outside shooting, and has shown a predilection for being in the right place at the right time. Unless countering a specific lineup, his minutes stay the same.

Shannon figures to be the first cut in playtime with the Big Ragu's return unless Finch expands his bench to ten. And yet, there are few players who could elevate TJ's game better than Donte. An attacking TJ off a Beringer screen with Donte, Ayo, and Trey spreading the floor is tailormade to confound defenses.

On those nights where the injury report is blank, I hope Finch keeps the pedal to the metal with frequent rotations in the vein of Memphis Grizzlies coach Tuomas Iisalo. The Grizz have 13 players averaging double digit minutes and only two players over 30 minutes a game, Cameron Boozer (32.3) and Ty Jerome (30.7).

The NBA season is grueling. We have seen year after year the Wolves struggle as the playoffs wear on. TJ, Bones, and Clark are good players, deserving of minutes that will keep the starters fresh for when they are needed most.

Look here for the inarguable answers through the first ten games.

The Wolves are presently top five in the league in the following team categories:

The Net Rating stat is leaning heavily on Minnesota's first three blow out wins. That said, they have only lost their games by a combined 17 points thus far. They are hitting plenty of threes. They are defending with energy and diving for loose balls. They don't treat the game as something that should be handed to them like some legacy Ivy Leaguer applying at his dad's company. They are battling for the ball and snatching it from less hungry competition.

Gone are the days of XL T-Shirts and Howl Towels. The Wolves have overloaded this season with all manner of tchotchke, curio and baseball jersey to lure fans and collectors alike to home games. Most of these do not have an image released but give you just enough information to send your imagination whirring.

There is an entire series of baseball hats with design help from former Wolves vets. For Kevin Garnett's jersey retirement, Minnesota has five unique pieces of career spanning collectible celebrating the Big Ticket's accomplishments wearing 21. There are bobbleheads, blankets, and backpacks and way way way too many baseball jerseys. And here they all are, definitively ranked.

There are seven ticket package giveaways featuring a baseball jersey this season. In collaboration with local artists, this is what the Wolves are doing for their Artist's Series this year. Each jersey, for a sport different than the one it is honoring, celebrates a societal cross-section; Latino Noche, Military Appreciation, Native American Heritage, Pride Night, Asian American and Pacific Islander Night, Black Excellence, and Inspiring Women.

I think the designs are fun. Each one is a variation with pin stripes in a variety of colors. Some of them have designs on the sleeve nodding to the theme of the night. All of them have "Wolves Basketball" on the back. And all of them are baseball jerseys.

I love the Artist's series. I have purchased at least one shirt each of the last two seasons. I love that a local artist gets to put their stamp on the Wolves design. I love that several of the local artists are BIPOC and women creators. I love that they came in a variety of T-shirts, sweatshirts, and hats.

I just don't understand the thought process in making seven different baseball jerseys. I don't know enough about production costs, or textiles, so forgive my potentially ignorant question, but, wouldn't a jersey with two less sleeves of material be cheaper while closer to the topic at hand? Can they not do basketball jerseys because of some contractual stuff with Nike? WHY!?

All that said, I think the Native American design is my favorite and I might need to get one.

The Wolves have played ten games in 17 days. If losing Ant and TJ wasn't enough, they have not had more than a day between games and twice have played in travel back-to-backs. All marathons are tough. Some like to remind you of that fact in the first few miles.

The giddy win streak to start the season, like those first marathon steps past gathered supporters, can make you feel invincible. Before you know it, you're running faster than you can sustain and its only mile two.

This is not to say that what we saw in the first three games is unsustainable, but with Ant out, the team is grasping for an identity while still playing fast and loose. LaMelo is trying to play aggressive defense and fouling like crazy.

The race is still young though. The stored ATP that let the Wolves sprint out of the gate may be spent, but they have years of experience and the benefits of youth. In the first full month of the season, they are searching for a pace they can maintain.

The challenge of racing a marathon is knowing the line between speed and overheating. The Wolves need to keep chasing after rebounds and through screens without losing anyone else to injury. If the news of Donte's return holds true, and Ant and TJ bounce back, they'll get an injection of energy better than any banana or unsavory gel packet found along the march.

On the challenging side of the opposition, Cooper Flagg looks incredible alongside the returned Kyrie Irving. The Mavericks are a deep squad and can hang around in any game. The Memphis Grizzlies, on the back of Ty Jerome's electric start and the connective play of rookie Cam Boozer are near the top of the conference.

Portland Trail Blazer's head coach Micah Nori returns to Minnesota for a home back-to-back. Nori has his team cooking, bolstered by Blazer legend, the renewed Damian Lillard.

With the Wolves only having one back to back in this stretch, and three days of rest between game 11 and 12 to rest and practice, I see the Wolves going into the month of December playing at the same pace, 14-6.

#2797. Our 3 takeaways after Kansas State football's pathetic showing vs Oklahoma State

MANHATTAN — Kansas State didn't even put up a fight as it was trounced by Oklahoma State, as the Wildcats' first season under Collin Klein continues to fall apart.

K-State lost 66-28 to the Cowboys on Saturday, Nov. 7, at Bill Snyder Family Stadium. It was the Wildcats' third consecutive loss. The 66 points allowed were the sixth most in Wildcats history.

The Wildcats (4-5, 1-5 Big 12) had no answers for Oklahoma State's offense when it was rolling. At the same time, the offense was ineffective and turned the ball over three times.

Here are our immediate takeaways from the Wildcats' latest loss.

The Wildcats knew they had a tall task when going up against Oklahoma State's offense, which features quarterback Drew Mestemaker, who could be the No. 1 overall pick in the upcoming NFL Draft.

The Cowboys scored touchdowns on their first four drives. They had four touchdown drives that only took three plays, with three of them spanning 64 yards or more. Oklahoma State had never scored more than 45 points in Manhattan, and had 49 at halftime.

Mestemaker was great, finishing with 313 passing yards and four scores, along with one receiving and one rushing touchdown. Cowboys running back Caleb Hawkins rushed for 175 yards and three scores.

Barnett was presented with an opportunity against what's been a bad Oklahoma State defense. In a potential dress rehearsal to show that he can be a starting quarterback at the Power 4 level, he was benched at halftime.

Barnett was ineffective, completing 7 of 17 passes for 106 yards, a touchdown and one interception. His touchdown came on a 73-yard pass to a wide-open Derrick Salley, who didn't have anyone within 15 yards of him in apparent busted coverage. It's clearer than ever that the heir-apparent to Avery Johnson, whether that's next year or in 2028, is not on this roster.

Dillon Duff relieved him in the second half, after it was Barnett who relieved him the week before at Colorado. He looked more comfortable than he did against Colorado, but it was in garbage time and against backups.

K-State is trending toward an off-season where the phrase "roster overhaul" might not do it justice. Yes, Johnson's availability would have made a difference in the previous two games he missed, but the defense isn't close to competitive.

At this point, it would be surprising to see Kansas State win another game. TCU could lie down next week amid a disappointing season, but K-State could do the same. Arizona should be a big favorite in Manhattan on Nov. 21, while the Wildcats will likely be an underdog at Iowa State to close the year.

What a disappointing year Klein's first season looks like it will turn out to be. He'll have to consider many tough decisions after this season.

Fox Sports' Rob Rang: Given the investment made in Drew Allar last spring, I don't believe the Steelers are planning to draft a quarterback in the first round of the 2027 draft. #2791. JJ Redick was pleased with ‘awesome’ season debut from Adou Thiero

One of the standouts of the early stages of the preseason was Adou Thiero, who looked to have built on a strong Summer League and was ready to be part of the Lakers' rotation.

However, an ill-timed injury halted Thiero's progress and kept him out of the opening weeks of the regular season. After some patience to allow swelling in his knee to go down, Thiero finally made his season debut in Friday's win over the Blazers and looked like he hadn't missed a beat from the preseason.

In only six minutes, Thiero's impact was felt as he tallied four points, four rebounds and two assists. After the game, head coach JJ Redick was asked about his performance and got rave reviews.

"I thought his first two defensive possessions, he made mistakes and then after that he was awesome," Redick said. "He literally did everything we asked him to do. He was great on the offensive glass. Even sometimes when we didn't necessarily get the possession, he was tapping the ball and crashing.

"I thought the read he made out of the short roll, I think they blitzed three times in the first half and two of those were against him. He makes the short roll and he gets the lob. I thought he played a great game and, defensively, he was really good in the second half."

Thiero came in late in the first quarter in the role previously held by Jarred Vanderbilt and immediately made an impact. Given his leaping ability, Thiero being the ball screener and roll man felt like an obvious fit.

The Blazers immediately tested him as they blitzed Luka Dončić, forcing Thiero to not just be in the right spot in the short roll, but then make a decision. He nailed both aspects, setting up Ziaire Williams for a dunk.

Shortly after, the Blazers opted for a more traditional pick-and-roll coverage. This time, Thiero rolled hard to the rim and caught the lob for an athletic finish.

"He did great," Walker Kessler said of Thiero. "Obviously, we value Adou a lot. He's a very physical player. Really talented, athletic player. I mean, that lob he caught is very, very impressive. He had a really good debut for the season."

Thiero's athleticism is unparalleled on the roster — and among the elites of the elite in the league as a whole — and offers the Lakers a different dynamic. Thiero as a screener and roller won't always work as it did on Friday, but his athleticism and activity level will continue to jump off the screen.

The Lakers' hope now is that he can stay healthy and start to stack positive performances in the regular season.

#2788. Early-season check-in on new Rockets Marcus Smart and Bogdan Bogdanovic

With the season being roughly one-tenth of the way through, I figured we could do a check-in on the two of the major offseason acquisitions, Bogdan Bogdanovic and Marcus Smart, who were signed to contracts paying them $3,524,115 and $6,064,00 this season, respectively.

Marcus Smart brings a lot more to the table for the Rockets than what appears in the box score. His defensive abilities, constant energy, and ability to make opposing guards miserable earned him Defensive Player of the Year honors in 2022. He brings another veteran presence to a young Rockets locker room. He will not be expected to score each night, but his ball-handling, shot creation, and the ability to make timely shots will make him a key piece of the Rockets' rotation.

So far this season, Marcus is averaging 9.8 points, 2.5 assists, 2.8 rebounds, and 1.3 steals while shooting 38.7% from three and 44.2% from the field. The field goal percentage is trending higher than his career average, as it three-point shooting, which is incredibly encouraging. Smart also had a stellar game vs. the Thunder, where he scored 24 points and made 7 three-pointers.

Houston needs perimeter shooting, and the 38% three-point shooter for his entire NBA career provides that. Bogdanovic can also create off the dribble at the second level of the offense and make shots when the main offensive players are on the bench or under heavy defensive pressure. He can create off the dribble at the second level of the offense and can make shots when the main offensive players are on the bench or under heavy pressure from the defense. This season, Bogdanovic is averaging 5.6 points per game, which does not seem like a lot, but he is shooting a blistering 45.5% from three. Any team can use that.

Bogdanovic is an excellent attacking addition to this year's sqaud. He can shoot, create off the dribble and space the floor, so he meets many of the Rockets' needs. However, his health and consistency will determine the effectiveness of this signing.

What is interesting about both of these acquisitions is the varying amounts of impact that each can bring to a game. Smart is brought in for his defense, energy, and leadership. Bogdanovic brings shooting, creation on offense, and floor spacing. Both players bring experience to Houston's young core and can help ease the transition of some of the young players into more rotation minutes as they continue to grow. They can be of use to players like Reed Sheppard by having veteran players on the team to help support the young players and to allow for more flexibility with lineups.

Ultimately, the value of both of these players will be determined by how they perform in games of consequence. Houston is trying to build a team of players that can help get them past the first round in the postseason, not just a collection of veterans and youngsters. If I had to give a grade for the two signings so far, I would give the Bogdonovic signing an A, and the Marcus Smart signing an A- only because Smart has missed time with an injury already.

Thats all for today! Make sure to let me know what you all think about the signings in the comments, and as always make sure to check back at The Dream Shake for all things Houston Rockets coverage.

#2786. Crown Jewel 2026 takeaways: WWE has an Oba Femi problem, and Roman Reigns is caught in the middle

WWE Crown Jewel 2026 went down Saturday at the ANB Arena in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, after weeks of questions over whether the event would actually take place. Roman Reigns and Chelsea Green won their respective Crown Jewel Championship matches, Tiffany Stratton cashed in her Money in the Bank briefcase on Green to claim the Women's World Championship, Oba Femi helped Penta and Je'Von Evans win the WWE World Tag Team titles, and Cody Rhodes defeated Randy Orton in a Last Man Standing match.

As we regroup before Survivor Series: WarGames in a few weeks, here's four big takeaways from Saturday's action in Saudi.

WWE's intention of keeping the spotlight on Oba Femi is borderline exhausting at this point.

It's clear he's WWE's next big star and they've done everything they can to ensure he's front and center as often as possible. The problem with much of the "Raw" scene over on Monday nights is that it's littered with guys WWE is actively trying to build up. So in positioning Femi as the next big star, he's just constantly hammering down on talents who haven't quite made it yet (see: Bron Breakker, Bronson Reed, etc) versus if he was on "SmackDown," where he'd be punching up at established veterans.

That was the case on Saturday yet again, where Femi was the difference-maker in Je'Von Evans getting his first taste of WWE gold alongside the men's Money in the Bank briefcase holder, Penta, by slamming Reed off the entrance ramp. For Evans, it's another step forward in establishing himself on the upper echelon of the "Raw" roster, while Penta bides his time with the briefcase with a pinfall victory over Austin Theory.

Absent the tag-team championship, it'll be interesting to see how Bron Breakker navigates the next steps in his career. He exploded back from injury, seemed well-positioned to claim a world championship, and has really coasted most of this year. His placement in a next big thing vs. next big thing match with Femi earlier this year was perhaps the highlight of his year, alongside a win over Seth Rollins. He still just hasn't found his footing though, and he runs the risk of following a similar path Jacob Fatu endured this year in climbing the ranks before empty booking brought him back to Earth.

The odds weren't great for Sami Zayn to leave Saturday's main event with a win, and Roman Reigns ultimately closed the door on any chance of that happening with a spear.

Despite the loss, this match at least did more to establish Zayn as a legitimate champion, following the old "sometimes losing is winning" trope. Zayn pushed Reigns to his limits before inevitably falling short, and received a respectful hug from the World Heavyweight Champion before exiting the ring. But no matter the offense Zayn pulled out in this one — and he did appear close at times to earning the win — it was written in the stars that he'd be on the losing end.

Zayn and Reigns picked up from their rivalry years ago in a really strong build to their showdown, but there's almost no question how the next six months should pan out. Reigns' sole purpose is to look as strong as humanly possible before dropping the title to Oba Femi at WrestleMania next year. Until April of next year, it's hard to imagine any challenger putting a real test to "The Tribal Chief."

That being said, Saturday's main event is another example of how, Femi, the champion in waiting, puts a serious gridlock on the title picture (and every Reigns match, for that matter) in a similar way WWE has notoriously fallen for, whether it was Cody Rhodes waiting a year to beat Reigns or one of the John Cena-The Rock WrestleMania tilts.

It makes Reigns champion by default and removes any elements of surprise that made wins like Zayn's world championship victories so spectacular. When you remove the surprise factor in wrestling, it becomes your favorite show that mailed it in for half of the year, absent almost any creativity. A Zayn loss also robbed fans of capitalizing on one of the best character developments in recent WWE television, which could've made him even more insufferable than he already is.

The endgame of Reigns vs. Femi at WrestleMania can still be the endgame, but what happens between now and then is one of the flattest lines WWE has drawn in some time.

Saturday's entire women's Crown Jewel match balanced between Liv Morgan being the proven, cocky champion, and Chelsea Green still working to prove she belonged despite having held the Women's World title since Money in the Bank. The formulaic approach panned out to a logical conclusion, after Morgan dismissed the Judgement Day and got caught in a roll-up to fall just short of the Women's Crown Jewel Championship.

As soon as Green got on the mic post-match, you just knew she'd be in trouble — and sure enough, Morgan's attack from behind set up a series of unfortunate events.

The perfect cherry on top was Tiffany Stratton hitting the ring and turning her back on Green with a briefcase hit to the head, forcing the champ to lose her title to a successful Money in the Bank cash-in.

Heel Stratton is perfect for "SmackDown" after incessantly trying to cash in her briefcase on Morgan to no avail. In a best-case scenario, the next month or so projects to follow Green playing a similar role as she did during Saturday's match, and proving she absolutely belongs in the title picture.

The story that's followed Cody Rhodes and Randy Orton since WrestleMania has been him pulling the trigger on punting his former mentor. Saturday's match was as brutal as expected, with intensity to open the bout and weapons quickly entering the fray.

Rhodes finished off Orton with a few Cross Rhodes — causing Orton's head to slam into the stairs — followed by the punt kick to keep the former world champ on the mat for the 10-count. The final sequence culminated months of build-up to the very moment Rhodes' foot slammed into Orton's head, and should now signal the end to their blood feud.

With the rest of the men's division essentially paired off, it'll be fascinating to see how Orton and Rhodes navigate their next steps.

For Rhodes, a return to the title picture seems like a logical path forward. He's sort of hovered right on the outskirts, occasionally finding his way into title matches since dropping the belt. But a fully-focused Rhodes promo about reclaiming his championship, while simultaneously competing in the upcoming John Cena Classic wouldn't be surprising.

With Orton unable to get back to his feet, there's less certainty about where he pops up next. My guess is he takes some time to heal before mixing it up with someone like Trick Williams.

#2785. Player Grades: Dallas gets on track against the Jazz with a 112-100 win

The Dallas Mavericks (5-4) took down the Utah Jazz (1-8), 112-100 on Friday night. The victory gets Dallas back on the right track after two-straight losses and gives the Mavs a 2-0 record in Emirates Cup play. Cooper Flagg and Kyrie Irving struggled a bit in the early going, but locked in down the stretch, while Morez Johnson, Jr. had the best game of his nascent NBA career.

We're switching it up this time and using a numerical grading system on a 10-point scale to grade the players. Let's get to the grades!

Irving was not sharp from the outset and had a difficult shooting night (7-of-20 overall; 0-of-3 from downtown). While that pulled down his grade, his all-out effort and hustle can't be overlooked. All night, Irving was on the floor lunging for steals, going amongst the trees for a couple of boards and hitting a few key shots in the latter part of the game to keep the Jazz at bay. It was not his best shooting night, but Irving made up for it in other ways, particularly on the defensive end.

Flagg shook off the massive funk he was in during the prior two games, but it took him until the second half to do so. He was 7-of-16 from the floor, with most of the misses coming in the first half and got completely lost on a couple of defensive sets, but he persisted. When it was all said and done, he nearly put up a triple-double. Three turnovers and 1-of-4 shooting from deep didn't help his grade, but this is the type of game that reminds you how special he is. He can have a rough half, yet end with a box score that looks great while having a true positive effect on the outcome of the game.

We try to show courtesy to all starters by featuring them in our Grades coverage, but Martin simply can't be graded. He missed a three-point attempt, committed two fouls and that's about it. He gets saved from an apparent 1/10 grade because he played so few minutes. Martin has been fine this year and contributes in ways that don't necessarily show in the box score, but one has to wonder if and when Zaccharie Risacher or Naji Marshall will start in his place.

Washington is like a new man this season, especially of late. He has played great ball and looks fully engaged over the past few games. His highlight was blocking a three-point attempt, picking up the rejected ball in stride and going in for a monster break-away slam to get the crowd into it.

He was all over the boards, led the team in plus/minus with a +20 and was within the flow of the game throughout. This was a coming out party that was great to witness.

Dallas needed a win after getting smacked by the Kings and losing a close one to the Spurs. #2779. NFL Week 9 predictions: 4 game picks for the Seahawks vs. Cardinals rematch

The Seattle Seahawks return to Lumen Field on Sunday to face the Arizona Cardinals in a divisional matchup with plenty of betting opportunities. Seattle enters as an 8.5-point favorite, with the game total set at 39.5 points, according to FanDuel Sportsbook.

The Seahawks have had an inconsistent season, but Arizona's defensive struggles create some interesting opportunities on both sides of the ball. The Cardinals have allowed 29 touchdowns through eight games, the most in the NFL. That could open the door for Seattle's offense, particularly in the red zone.

Here are four bets/game picks worth considering ahead of Sunday's game.

Jadarian Price is an interesting option to find the end zone against Arizona. The rookie has shown the potential to turn an ordinary running lane into a big play, and Seattle's recent investment in its offensive line could help him find more opportunities to showcase that ability.

Against a defense that has struggled throughout the season, those opportunities could translate into a touchdown.

There is one important caveat, though: Price needs to take better care of the football. His fumbles have been a concern, and another mistake could limit his opportunities. If he can protect the ball, his explosiveness gives him a legitimate chance to make an impact on the scoreboard.

Trey McBride is one of the most reliable pass-catching tight ends in the NFL, and Seattle has historically struggled to contain him. The coverage behind Seattle's linebackers has been a recurring issue, particularly when opponents attack the intermediate areas of the field.

McBride is exactly the type of player who can take advantage of that weakness. He's a dependable target, consistently finds space in coverage and gives his quarterback a reliable option when the pocket gets uncomfortable. Arizona should have plenty of reasons to involve him throughout the game, especially if Seattle prioritizes preventing explosive plays elsewhere.

Jaxon Smith-Njigba should be one of Drew Lock's most important weapons on Sunday. The two have shown good chemistry, and that connection could become particularly valuable against an Arizona defense that has struggled to consistently defend the passing game.

Smith-Njigba can help Seattle address one of its biggest offensive concerns: finishing drives in the red zone. He was an important part of the solution in the first meeting between these teams, and the Seahawks should look to get him involved again when the field becomes shorter.

His value isn't limited to the red zone, either. Smith-Njigba has also been a dangerous deep threat throughout the season, capable of creating separation and turning downfield opportunities into explosive plays. That versatility makes him an especially valuable target for Lock, who will need reliable options to keep the offense moving.

With their established chemistry and JSN's ability to contribute at every level of the field, there's a good case for backing him to find the end zone.

This might be the most difficult bet to evaluate, largely because of the uncertainty surrounding Drew Lock. However, I don't see much of a middle ground in this matchup.

If Lock struggles, Seattle could have a difficult afternoon. Turnovers, particularly interceptions, could give Arizona short fields and keep the Cardinals in a game where they might otherwise struggle to keep pace offensively.

On the other hand, Lock could deliver another performance similar to his first meeting against Arizona. If he protects the football, establishes a rhythm with Smith-Njigba and takes advantage of Seattle's improved offensive line, the Seahawks have enough talent to win comfortably and cover the spread.

The Cardinals' defensive struggles make the second scenario entirely possible. Seattle has the weapons to create separation on the scoreboard, but everything depends on which version of Lock shows up.

I'm willing to take the risk because I believe Seattle has a significant advantage if its quarterback plays a clean game.

#2777. 'A shared vision': LASA boys pace each other to Class 5A UIL state cross-country title

ROUND ROCK - Over two cool, breezy days at Old Settler's Park, more than 1,500 of the state's best high school distance runners competed in the UIL state cross-country championships. And while there were a number of standout performances from Central Texas runners, it was Austin's LASA Raptors who rose to the pinnacle, capturing first place in Saturday's Class 5A race.

The Raptors were led by senior Liam Brandyberry, who finished seventh overall in 15 minutes, 28 seconds on the rolling 5K course.

"It took preparation, drive, commitment, character and courage to do what they had to do today, which is not easy," LASA head cross-country coach Mary Beth Metcalf said of the boys team, which also consisted of seniors Joaquin Gonzalez, John Wilson, Cruz Alcorta and Hugo Radjef, and juniors Ben Vazquez and Sam Smith.

"Not so much a tactical approach, it was more about being committed to one another," Metcalf added. "During the race, when it feels overwhelming, when they feel like maybe they can't hang on any longer, when their brains are telling them to let up, I ask them to think about one another and the love that they have for their teammates, and to let that teammate commitment be what drives them forward. Our team has a shared commitment and obligation to will it into reality. It's a shared vision."

Only the top five runners from each team have their finishing places added together to calculate the team score; the team with the lowest total score wins. LASA scored 94 points, ahead of runner-up Weslaco East's 98 and third-place Dallas Wilson's 113. Weslaco East's Alexander Nava won the overall race in 15 minutes, 13 seconds, while Georgetown's Matthew Morales averaged 4:56 per mile to grab second in 15:18. Liberty Hill's Zander Radziwon was 11th (15:40) and Lockhart's Ethan Herrera (15:52) was 19th.

"These boys, since they've been freshmen, they've always felt like a team and worked together like a team," LASA principal Stacia Crescenzi said. "What makes this so emotional today is not that they won, but that they did it together."

In Friday's Class 6A meet, Vandegrift's Avinash Dewagan had a lot of momentum leading up to the state meet after winning both the district and Region III-6A meets and it continued at state. The sophomore took second overall (14:39) behind Denton Guyer's nationally-ranked junior, Ruel Newberry (14:36).

El Paso Eastwood won the 6A boys race ahead of Southlake Carroll and Keller.

"Coming in second to Newbury is a pretty big deal," Vandegrift coach Colin Sully said. "No question, Avinash pulled our team to fifth place. Though we placed second here at state the past four years, I'm happy with how the boys team ran today."

Flower Mound won the 6A girls race ahead of Conroe The Woodlands and Southlake Carroll. The Vandegrift girls, led by senior Caroline Krupa, placed 11th.

In addition to Dewagan, Round Rock's Andrew Esparza also ran a solid race, taking sixth in 14:52. Other notable finishers included Bowie's Cooper Ford (22nd in 15:34), and Round Rock's Zachary Stevens (25th in 15:39). Lake Travis' Olivia Laudicina was the top Central Texas girls finisher in Class 6A, coming in 17th (18:22). Stony Point's Sophia Lopez placed 22nd in 18:29.

#2776. Ranking the top 50 MLB free agents for the 2026-27 offseason, plus landing spots for every player

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The World Series is complete, the Milwaukee Brewers are first-time champions and MLB's offseason is already underway. It won't be long until the hot stove sizzles.

To get the winter started, CBS Sports has ranked the top 50 MLB free agents for the 2026-27 offseason. These rankings are compiled through statistical and video analysis, past market research, plus vibes and general hunches. We have included players expected to make the leap from Japan's NPB and South Korea's KBO to the big leagues, but not non-tender candidates or unexpected option decisions.

Of course, this is no normal offseason. With the current collective bargaining agreement set to expire at 11:59 p.m. on Dec. 1, a lockout is all but certain. How long will it last? What will baseball -- and for our purposes, contracts -- look like on the other side? Will teams and players rush to make deals before the work stoppage or delay everything until it's over? Who knows. These are the ultimate questions of the winter, and how they get answered is up to the owners and the players' union.

The two most important things to know about these rankings: First, free agency is forward-looking. What you've done in the past counts for only so much. More than ever before, teams pay players based on what they expect them to do in the future, not what they've done in their career to date. These rankings are intended to reflect that.

And second, the least important part of this exercise is the potential landing spots listed for each player. There are more than three suitors for almost every player, and it's not intended as a snub if your team isn't listed here. Here now are our top 50 free agents.

Excluding Yoshinobu Yamamoto, who was a special case as a Japanese star with no MLB track record, Skubal is the best starting pitcher to hit free agency since Gerrit Cole in 2019. He showed few long-lasting effects from the NanoScope elbow surgery in May and remains a capital-A Ace with terrific surface stats and under-the-hood performance indicators. Skubal brings four swing-and-miss pitches to the table (four-seamer, changeup, slider, curveball), a near MLB-best ability to limit exit velocity, and elite strike-throwing ability (MLB's third-lowest walk rate since 2023). Build an ace starter in a lab and he would look a lot like Skubal. He'll play the entire 2027 season at age 30, and given the things teams can do with pitchers these days, Skubal figures to remain a frontline starter for most of a long-term contract. He's the only true balance-of-power player available in free agency this offseason. Skubal can swing a division race and a postseason series all by himself.

Morejon won't turn 28 until late February and is one of the youngest free agents available. He has been one of the game's best relievers the last three years, one who can miss bats and limit hard-hit ability at near MLB-best levels, plus you need not shelter him against right-handed batters. Morejon is a bona fide late-inning reliever who happens to throw left-handed. As good as he is out of the bullpen, it seems likely an enterprising team will give him a chance to start in 2027, and Morejon doesn't just have a chance to make it work. He has a chance to be an excellent starter thanks to his premium four-pitch mix (four-seamer, sinker, slider, changeup) and the fact he sits right at 100 mph. Morejon can give some velocity back while working longer outings and still have plenty in the tank to miss bats in the strike zone. And if starting doesn't work, he can go right back to dominating as a reliever. This ranking reflects my belief in Morejon as a starter. There is one potential red flag: Morejon was not available in Games 2-4 of the NLDS with what Padres manager Craig Stammen called "stickiness" in his shoulder. Interested teams will no doubt closely scrutinize Morejon's medicals.

Rogers was never able to fully work off the early season stinkers that inflated his ERA, though this is free agency, and ERA is close to the last thing on the minds of interested teams. You're looking forward in free agency, not backward. The underlying performance indicators are very strong, specifically the ability to get chase and avoid the barrel with four pitches (four-seamer, sinker, changeup, sweeper) that light up analytical models. Rogers also has a fifth-pitch cutter and has shown the ability to hammer the strike zone the last two years. There are some lefty Zack Wheeler vibes here. When Wheeler became a free agent after 2019, he already had the analytical stamp of approval, and the belief was he could get to another level with fine-tuning and good health. That is exactly what happened. Lefty Wheeler would obviously be the best-case scenario outcome for Rogers, but the bottom line is he will play the entire 2027 season at age 29, and he throws strikes with four pitches that the pitch data models already consider above average. More than a few teams will undoubtedly see Rogers as a pitcher who is a tweak or two away from finding another gear.

The Hanshin Tigers will post Sato for MLB teams this offseason, the NPB club announced in late October. He will play the entire 2027 season at age 28 and is coming off a .306/.383/.609 slash line with 39 home runs, which won him Japan's first Triple Crown since Munetaka Murakami in 2022. Sato has a similar skill set but is not quite Murakami 2.0. He doesn't have quite as much power (but has plenty of it) and won't walk nearly as often, but he does swing and miss a bunch and is unlikely to remain at the hot corner long-term. Sato is a very aggressive hitter who ran a 66% contact rate this past season. That is below the 77% MLB average. The consensus seems to be that he will land at first base or in a corner outfield spot if not next year, then soon. Murakami successfully overcame his contact issues to slug 35 homers in only 127 games around a hamstring injury. At minimum, that will have MLB teams reconsidering how they evaluate the Japan-to-MLB transition. Like Murakami, Sato carries risk, and like Murakami, his power makes that risk worth the dice roll.

It has been a roller coaster year for Peralta, who flopped with the Mets, rebounded with the Rays, then faced the Brewers (his former team) in the World Series and lost. The post-deadline stint with Tampa salvaged Peralta's free agent year. They made several adjustments, most notably raising his arm angle and getting him to pitch exclusively from the stretch, and the result was a livelier fastball and also better command. He's still five-and-fly Freddy. Even the best version of Peralta won't pitch deep into games and can be a tough watch because he nibbles and throws so many pitches per inning. They tend to be good innings, though, and the guy never misses a start. Worst case, Peralta is a mid-rotation starter you can count on to take the ball every fifth day. The best case is someone who can front a contender's rotation. Fastball Freddy was always going to be a great bounceback candidate this offseason. The Rays just beat everyone to it at the trade deadline.

In what was his worst season as a hitter since his rookie year in 2021, Chisholm was still a league-average bat in 2026, and his top-shelf defense and baserunning still landed him at 3.5 WAR. Chisholm is a style-over-substance player who is not for everyone, but his second base defense and near-MLB-best baserunning skills give him a very high floor. He's a reasonable bet for 20-ish home runs with the potential to go 30-30, and Chisholm has improved his plate discipline enough to run walk rates north of 10% the last two years. The downside is his propensity to swing and miss. Chisholm has posted below-average in-zone contact rates throughout his career and contact rates that low always come with risk. That risk is mitigated somewhat by the secondary skills (defense, etc.) and the fact that Chisholm will play the entire 2027 season at age 29. You probably don't want him as your best or second-best player, but he's also an overqualified No. 6-7 hitter who brings so much else to the table.

The 32-year-old Suzuki is one of only four qualified hitters to post a 125 OPS+ or better each of the last four seasons. He's a right-handed hitter with unerring patience and strong ball-tracking data (exit velocity, etc.) at a time when right-handed power is in shockingly short supply. Suzuki is also sneaky fast, though don't expect him to pile up big stolen base totals. Thanks to improved jumps with the help of outfield coach Quintin Berry, Suzuki made the leap from average at best defender to legitimately excellent this season. The team that signs him will likely be the team that believes his defensive improvement is sticky. Even if it isn't, Suzuki's righty thump is a scarce commodity these days, and will land him a nice contract even as he prepares to enter his mid-30s. At worst, you'll get a power-and-patience hitter who is comfortable playing in the spotlight.

King has reportedly already opted out of the final two years and $58 million remaining on his contract and he should have no trouble beating that this offseason, even if it is more total dollars over more years but at a lower annual salary. King is a five-pitch righty with an extreme east/west attack -- the movement on King's sinker, sweeper, and changeup border on cartoonish -- who makes his living by limiting hard contact more than he does missing bats and blowing hitters away. He has consistently outperformed the various ERA estimators (FIP, xERA, etc.) throughout his career, and when you do it over hundreds of innings, it's a skill, not a fluke. King will turn 32 in May and his fastball is getting hit a little harder with each passing year. There is some blow-up potential here. Still, King is a high-end No. 2 starter and he's regarded as a Grade-A clubhouse guy, which is not nothing. He's instantly become a fan favorite wherever he's played.

Always a strong hitter, Arozarena had a career-best season in 2026, during which he hit offspeed pitches (changeups, splitters, etc.) better than ever. His superpower has always been his ability to punish fastballs and breaking balls at above-average rates. Now he added the "hit soft stuff" club to his bag. Arozarena will play the entire 2027 season at age 32 and he offers righty thump at a time when it's very hard to find, plus he's shown time and time again that he is unafraid of big moments. He'll also chip in 20-plus steals despite a lack of blazing speed. The downside is Arozarena is basically a DH at this point in his career. Poor jumps, poor routes, poor range, poor arm. He's a liability in the outfield and whichever team signs him would be wise to DH him exclusively.

Over the last four seasons, Jeffers has reduced his strikeout rate from 27.8% to 20.2% to 19.6% to an excellent 17.9% in 2026. He opened his stance a little and moved further back in the box a few years ago, felt good about it, and has continued to open and widen his stance a tiny bit more with each passing year. Jeffers offers right-handed pull power and strong plate discipline to go with his continually improving contact skills. The downside is his defense behind the plate, which grades out poorly every which way. Blocking, throwing, framing, etc. The offensive bar at catcher is on the floor. Jeffers clears it with plenty of room to spare, enough that teams will overlook the shaky glovework. He will turn 30 in June and is the best catcher to hit free agency since Willson Contreras in 2022.

Arraez continues to hum along, posting Dead Ball Era contact rates while making fans of every team wish they had him. Offensively, he's the same player he's always been. Arraez is the game's best bat-to-ball guy. He'll contend for a batting title, hit single-digit home runs, and rarely walk because he so easily puts the ball in play. How much do you buy into his improvement in the field? Arraez might have been the single worst defensive player in baseball prior to 2026, then he worked with infield guru Ron Washington with the Giants and became a legitimately above-average defender at second base. Above average according to both the eye test and the numbers, which isn't always the case with defense. If you think that defensive improvement is real, you see a 4-WAR player who will turn only 30 soon after Opening Day. If you don't, you see a one-tool player who barely scraped 1 WAR in 2024 and 2025. Don't be surprised if Arraez again has trouble drumming up interest as a free agent.

Rake Bauers (finally) lived up to the nickname this year and carried it over into the postseason, particularly during the NLCS. Long an exit velocity and hard-hit rate darling, Bauers fully tapped into his power in 2026 thanks to a more open stance and moving back in the box and further off the plate. That allowed him to see the ball better and get his bat into the hitting position on time more consistently. I'm not 100% sold on those adjustments solving his career-long issues with lefties, though at least there is a tangible reason to believe in his great left-on-left performance this season. Bauers can be an adventure in the field (he has played outfield in the past) and he just turned 31. A few teams will look for the next Jake Bauers rather than pay the actual Jake Bauers.

There is no doubting Lowe's power. He's hit well over 30 homers per 600 plate appearances throughout his career. There simply aren't many middle infielders who hit the ball over the fence that consistently, and those who can are infrequently available. Prior to 2026, Lowe was close to a one-tool player, but he made huge gains in the field thanks to Pittsburgh's coaching staff. How huge? Lowe went from -14 outs above average in 2025 to +15 in 2026. It's the largest year-over-year improvement in Statcast history. The power has always been real and the defensive improvement is encouraging. The downsides are near-bottom-of-the-league contact rates, a declining walk rate, a lengthy injury history, and the fact that Lowe is already 32. That all adds up to an uncomfortable amount of collapse risk.

Gray has reportedly mulled retirement over the last few offseasons, but he intends to pitch in 2027. He's as crafty as ever, using six pitches regularly and giving hitters every look. Hard, soft, sharp break, big movement, etc. Gray's stuff works in such a way that he seems to get a quick first or second pitch out every inning, allowing him to pitch deep into games. He completed six innings 22 times in his 29 starts this past season, which makes him a workhorse by 2026 standards. Gray will pitch the entire 2027 season at age 37 and he's lost enough velocity to shrink his margin of error meaningfully, which creates some over-the-cliff risk. Still, the 14-year veteran is not out of place as the No. 2 starter in a postseason rotation.

Being boring is an underrated closer trait and Bednar, 32, has it. He won't beat himself with walks, he limits hard contact, he misses bats, he's effective against righties and lefties, and he proved he's built for the postseason and big markets during his time in New York. His low-90s splitter is an equalizer that seems impossible to square up. Furthermore, Bednar is a low-maintenance pitcher who's shown a willingness to go multiple innings and work as a setup man. He won't make a stink about his role. There has been some age-related velocity loss and he had to abandon his curveball at times this past season because he had so much trouble commanding it. Otherwise, Bednar is a plug-and-play high-leverage reliever.

Every contender could use a player like Dubón. He's a true super utility guy who can play every position except catcher -- and play it well. Offensively, Dubón is an aggressive bat-to-ball player with a knack for ideal launch angles, which, in English, means he's a line drive hitter. He obliterated his previous career high in games played and plate appearances this past season and handled the workload well. Dubón is older than you may realize (he turns 33 in July), but he's been valuable everywhere he's played, and he's the kind of player every manager loves. The ability to play everywhere, put the ball in play, and be relentlessly upbeat is the ideal modern utility man.

Offensively, Happ has "old player skills." He has always walked a lot, which keeps his on-base percentage respectable even as his batting average has taken a hit. You can also pencil him in for 20-25 homers. Dingers and discipline typically age well. Defensively, Happ remains Gold Glove-caliber thanks to a great first step and a strong arm. He won't wow you with highlight reel catches, but he will catch everything he's supposed to catch and then some. Happ will play most of next season at age 32 and there has been enough slippage in his contact rates and exit velocity that I'm comfortable calling them worrisome. Age-related decline might be right around the corner, though the skill set suggests a gentle decline rather than a complete collapse. I have more faith in Happ being a steady contributor over the next one or two years than some position players ranked above him. There's just less upside.

It is incorrect to say Iglesias was as good as ever in 2026. He was terrific, to be sure, but the contact allowed is getting louder and he's lost two ticks off his fastball the last two years. That is a normal baseball thing for someone who has a big career workload (for a reliever) and will pitch all of next season at age 37. Iglesias has closer chops and his changeup is one of the very best pitches in the sport, and all you need as a one-inning reliever is that one great pitch. At this age, there's always a chance it all comes crashing down. Iglesias will -- and should -- continue to get well-paying one-year contracts until that happens.

Listed at 5-foot-8, Taira gets outlier extension down the mound (close to seven feet despite his height), which creates a low release window. Hitters rarely see the ball come from where Taira releases it. He's not a gimmick pitcher either. Taira sits mid-90s with his four-seam fastball and backs it up with a cutter, sinker, sweeper, slider, changeup, and splitter. The sweeper and slider are distinct pitches, as are the changeup and splitter. The Seibu Lions used Taira as a reliever in 2024 and 2025, then started him in 2026, and he handled the assignment well. The breaking balls are just OK, and the fact of the matter is that pitchers this height don't often hold up under a starter's workload. I would assume the team that signs Taira will give him a chance to start. In the long run, though, he might be a reliever, perhaps even a multi-inning setup man. Seibu announced on Oct. 30 that Taira will be posted this offseason.

Long a pitch data darling, Mahle had the best stretch of his career after joining the Braves at the trade deadline. They ramped up his splitter usage and tweaked his slider a tad, and also got him to live in the shadows of the strike zone more often. Mahle will not continue posting a 1.99 ERA. No one is that good. He has always passed the analytical test, though, and he's finally healthy after arm injuries limited him to 125 innings from 2023-25. Health will always be a question. That's just the way it is with pitchers who've gotten hurt repeatedly. Mahle just turned 32, though, and we finally saw proof of concept this year. This deep into the free agent rankings, every pitcher carries some kind of risk. I like Mahle's upside more than the rest.

A bad luck broken leg (he was hit by a comebacker) derailed Holmes in 2026. He got hurt in May, was traded while on the injured list, then returned in August without his usual velocity. Even while working in the low 90s rather than mid-90s, Holmes remained one of the game's very best ground ball artists. His sweeper and cutter are above-average weapons according to the pitch data models, and Holmes picked up a nice kick-change with the Mets. It's not everything, but teams will like that Holmes is postseason and big-market battle-tested following his time with the two New York teams, and that he has experience as a starter and a reliever. The ground balls give Holmes a reasonably high floor. He's very likely to be useful in some capacity in 2027, and it helps that he's regarded as coachable and a strong teammate. The declining velocity, declining strikeout rate, and the fact that Holmes will pitch all of next season at age 34 will chill his market a bit.

Velocity is important for every pitcher and that is especially true for Gausman. He's made a living throwing fastballs almost literally down the middle to set up his all-world splitter. Hitters chase the splitter because they think it's a fastball and take the fastball for strikes because they sit on the splitter. When Gausman sat 95-96 mph at his peak, he dominated. Now that he's closer to 93-94 mph most nights, it doesn't work quite as well. He toyed with a sweeper late in the season and I would expect the team that signs him to hone in on that pitch (or some other breaking ball) to mitigate the velocity loss. Gausman will pitch the entire 2027 season at age 36 and he's as good a bet to make 32 starts next year as any pitcher in the game, which is not nothing.

France has reinvented himself a few times over the years and the current version is the best version yet. He opened his stance a bit this season and the result was much more hard contact, specifically against fastballs. France has always posted solid contact and walk rates. Now, he's getting his bat through the zone a little quicker and producing more on contact. Also, France has made himself into an excellent defensive first baseman. One of the very best in the game, in fact. His track record as a top hitter is one year, basically, and France will turn 33 next summer. The dearth of quality right-handed bats could still land him a multi-year contract.

You can talk yourself into Mize, 30 in May, having untapped upside as a former No. 1 overall draft pick who pitched pretty well this past season around a series of groin injuries before being traded to San Diego at the deadline. You can also talk yourself into Mize being fool's gold because he doesn't have a plus pitch, frequents the injured list, and hasn't impressed despite pitching in pitcher-friendly ballparks his entire career. The things teams can do with pitchers these days are amazing, really. I would never rule out a prime-aged pitcher figuring things out and carving out a strong second phase to his career. Eventually, though, the shine of the "former No. 1 overall pick" thing wears off.

May turned only 29 in September and he's topped 130 innings in back-to-back years after throwing 101 innings total around injuries, including UCL surgery, from 2021-24. Even after the injuries, May still lives in the mid-to-upper-90s with his sinker, and pitch data models are fond of his sweeper and curveball. It is not the best sign, though, that the Brewers, who know pitching as well as any team, couldn't fully unlock May after making him their big deadline rotation addition. Still, the combination of age and high-octane stuff makes him a nice upside play on a short-term contract, particularly for a rebuilding team that is willing to run him out there every fifth day regardless of results.

A down 2026 season took some of the shine off Itoh, who won the 2025 Eiji Sawamura Award (Japan's Cy Young equivalent) after throwing 196 ⅔ innings with a 2.52 ERA. To be sure, Itoh pitched well in 2026 (3.18 ERA in 172 ⅔ innings), but he was not as consistently dominant as in the past. The 5-foot-9 right-hander is a seven-pitch pitcher with a low-90s fastball and the usual array of secondary pitches (sinker, cutter, curveball, slider, sweeper, splitter), none of which stands out as a plus offering. Itoh has thrown at least 150 innings in each of the last six seasons. He's seen as a crafty back-end starter in MLB, or perhaps even a reliever (Itoh sat 96 mph out of the bullpen in the World Baseball Classic). The Hokkaido Nippon Ham Fighters are expected to post Itoh, who turned 29 in August, this winter.

The only question is health. Soroka's 116 innings this season were his most since his National League Rookie of the Year runner-up season in 2019. Back then, Soroka was a sinker specialist and ground ball machine. These days, he's a low-to-mid-90s four-seam fastball guy with a slurvy breaking ball that falls somewhere between a curveball and a slider. Soroka also has a cutter, a changeup, and, yep, still the sinker. The breaking ball grades out as his best pitch, though everything plays up because he tunnels well and is a good strike-thrower. I like Soroka, who will pitch most of next season at 29, more as a reliever, possibly even as a multi-inning high-leverage guy. The skill set is that of a back-end starter though, and you needn't squint too much to see upside beyond that.

The Nationals did terrific work signing Griffin to a low-cost one-year contract ($5.5 million) last offseason. He had an All-Star first half, then Washington flipped him for four prospects at the trade deadline. Griffin added about three pitches during his three years with the Yomiuri Giants in Japan and now is one of baseball's few true seven-pitch pitchers. He's an extreme strike-thrower and Griffin tunnels his pitches in such a way that his entire arsenal punches above its weight. There isn't one or two individual pitches that stand out, but they all work together well. Griffin will turn 32 in July and he's built for a full season's workload. He may not have the upside you can dream on like a few pitchers ranked ahead of him, but Griffin feels like a decent bet to be a top 75-ish starter in 2027 as long as he stays healthy.

Martinez, 36, posted the lowest strikeout rate among qualified pitchers in 2026, and also the 14th-lowest ERA. He's traded whiffs for weak contact the last few years and, frankly, I don't think you can reasonably expect him to post baseball's fourth-lowest ground ball rate and sixth-lowest home run rate again next season. Those are two things that rarely go together, even with Martinez's propensity for weak contact. His high arm angle creates an unusual look for hitters and creates tremendous downward action on his sinker and changeup. Martinez also has a cutter and a curveball. He made 31 starts and threw 180 innings for the Rays this year, so he can be a regular member of the rotation, if needed. Moving forward, Martinez might be most valuable as the high-end swingman he was from 2022-25.

There are days when Imanaga looks like an ace and days when he simply can't keep the ball in the park. He's an extreme fly ball pitcher who has averaged one homer every 4 ⅔ innings or so the last two years. Imanaga regained the tick of velocity he lost in 2025, but we're still talking about a pitcher who lives in the 91-93 mph range most days. It's an upshoot fastball, meaning it gets a lot of empty swings at the top of the zone thanks to his arm angle and release height, but when Imanaga misses his spot, he pays a big price. His splitter and sweeper are good enough secondary pitches. Imanaga will pitch most of next season at age 33 and he's a pitching nerd who is willing to tinker, which perhaps gives him a chance to reshape his arsenal as he gets into his mid-30s.

31. LHP JoJo Romero32. RHP Jonathan Loáisiga 33. RHP Paul Blackburn 34. RHP Evan Phillips 35. LHP Alex Vesia

An appendectomy split Romero's season in two. He was great during the Brewers' postseason run and has been one of the game's better lefty relievers for four years now. His sinker/sweeper attack is plenty good enough that Romero does not have to be sheltered against righties. Loáisiga had his first healthy season in four years and got back to throwing upper-90s bowling ball sinkers. He won't miss many bats at this point in his career, but he will generate a ton of weak contact on the ground. A good defensive infield is a must behind him. Blackburn thrived in his first season as a full-time reliever and, like Loáisiga, he did it with a weak ground ball contact rate rather than strikeouts. He pitches like a starter in relief in that he uses five pitches regularly, and held up across multi-inning outings all season. Phillips ran into some home run trouble when he first returned from Tommy John surgery in July, but otherwise continued to rack up whiffs with his fastball/sweeper combo. Vesia's fastball is mostly 90-91 mph these days and he walks too many batters, but he is fearless, and he can still get his heater by hitters at the top rail thanks to the movement traits.

36. 2B Gleyber Torres 37. C Carson Kelly38. 1B/3B Alec Bohm 39. UTIL Edmundo Sosa40. OF Michael Conforto   41. DH George Springer

These days, Torres is a contact/walks guy who might hit 15 homers and provide what can charitably be described as below-average defense and baserunning. He is not out of place as a contender's leadoff hitter given his on-base ability, though it's name value more than one-field value at this point. Kelly may be ranked too low here given his last two seasons and the general lack of quality catchers in free agency. He's an above-average contact/plate discipline guy with limited hard-hit ability and an unfortunate knack for ground ball contact. Defensively, Kelly moves well below the plate but is not much of a framer or thrower. He fits best as a platoon or half-time catcher, not as the undisputed starter. Bohm has solid contact quality data and a history of hitting lefties hard. He can play first and third bases in the sense that he can stand at first and third base, but you won't like what you see. Bohm has been miscast as a middle-of-the-order hitter and everyday third baseman over the last few years. The 30-year-old has real value as a righty platoon bat, though. Sosa had a down year at the plate despite no change under the hood (exit velocity, etc.). He has a long track record of hammering lefties, plus you can put him almost anywhere on the field. Every team could use a bench guy like that. Conforto showed very promising underlying data during his miserable 2025 and turned it into results in 2026. He's a nifty lefty platoon guy at this point in his career. Springer's resurgence in 2025 did not carry over into 2026. He'll play all of next season at age 37 and there isn't much juice left in his bat. The sport's lack of quality right-handed bats could get him a job with a contender, though he needs to DH regularly to stay healthy and productive.

42. CF Daulton Varsho 43. RHP Nick Pivetta 44. RHP Shane Bieber 45. LHP Kris Bubic 46. C Tyler Stephenson

September wrist surgery bumps Varsho down these rankings even though he's the best defensive center fielder in free agency. The ball-tracking data (exit velocity, etc.) is below average and he is not a disciplined hitter. You can dream on Varsho returning to his 2025 form, but, with his 31st birthday coming up next year, the more likely outcome is a glove-first player who fights to a draw as a league-average hitter and posts an on-base percentage that starts with a 2. Pivetta missed most of this season with a flexor injury and that triggered a clause that gives the Padres the option to walk away from the two years and $32 remaining on his contract. I'm not 100% convinced it will happen, but it is possible. Pivetta will turn 34 in February and will need his stuff to play better than it did after the injury to make postseason starts in 2027. Injuries, including Tommy John surgery, have limited Bieber to 108 innings over the last three years, and he made only 11 wobbly starts in 2026. He will turn 32 in May and his command is so exceptional that he can survive with the low-90s velocity he showed this summer, but it is a tightrope walk these days. Bubic has an outlier fastball thanks to its rise and his unusual release point. Giving him a chance to start for the last two years was a worthwhile experiment, though the persistent arm injuries likely mean it's time to put a pin in that and turn him back into a full-time reliever. Stephenson has all-fields power and checks analytical boxes with his hard-hit data. He is in the conversation for the worst defensive catcher in the sport, though. A team with a good catching development program might convince themselves they can coach him up to average defense.

47. LHP Matthew Boyd 48. LHP David Peterson 49. LHP Robbie Ray50. LHP Patrick Sandoval

Boyd will pitch all of next season at 36 and his package of secondary pitches is unique given the movement and his arm angle. He is fearless and could maybe benefit from throwing fewer strikes. Boyd has the stuff to get chases, and his mistakes in the zone tend to leave the yard. The Cubs got Peterson's career back on the rails following a June trade. Much of that was pitch sequencing and playing in front of the best defense in baseball. The 31-year-old's upside is a No. 4-5 starter you can pencil in for 20-something starts. Ray's season went downhill after his trade to San Diego. His stuff is down several ticks from his prime and his strikeout rate has cratered now that he's in his mid-30s. If you need someone to throw 110 pitches to get 13-15 outs every fifth day, he's your guy. Sandoval did not have the smoothest return from Tommy John surgery this season, though I am curious to see what he looks like as he gets further away from surgery. He showed some good secondary pitch shapes and an ability to keep the ball on the ground. I reckon he'll outperform at least a few of the pitchers we have ranked ahead of him in 2027.
