#2775. 2026-27 NHL season predictions: Expert picks for Stanley Cup playoffs, champion and major awards this season

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Following a brief offseason and an expedited preseason, the 2026-27 NHL season has arrived. Before the puck drops on opening night, we have some predictions to make.

If this season feel like it's staring earlier than usual, that's because it is. The NHL is adopting an 84-game regular season, which just means more hockey for the rest of us. That also means a long and arduous journey to the Stanley Cup is ever so slightly more difficult.

So, what will that journey look like? The Carolina Hurricanes are looking to defend their title as Cup champions, but they'll have to contend with a deep Eastern Conference and some real juggernauts in the Western Conference. With that in mind, we logged our expert predictions for the playoff field in each conference -- and there were a few surprises -- before making our Stanley Cup Final selections.

We also called our shot on the winners of each major individual award. Connor McDavid is looking for his fourth Hart Trophy, but he's got some competition from an up-and-coming superstar in his own division. Races for the Norris Trophy and Vezina Trophy should be pretty wide open, and unexpected candidates always emerge throughout the season.

It should be a fun season in the NHL, so follow along with all our coverage at CBS Sports. Let's get things kicked off with the season preview and predictions, which will of course be 100% accurate.

Baumgartner: I don't see many new faces entering the conversation when it comes to the Eastern Conference playoff race. A healthy Florida Panthers side will slot themselves right back towards the top of the Atlantic, and a revamped Washington Capitals side should be able to make some noise in the Metropolitan. Besides that, I have six 2026 playoff teams returning to the dance in 2027.

Nivison: As much as I hate to go with chalk in preseason predictions -- because it rarely happens that way -- there's no denying the top dogs in the West. The Avalanche and Stars are the class of the Central Division, and the Golden Knights should pound a pitiful Pacific Division into a pulp. Things get more interesting behind those clear Cup contenders, and I'm projecting another significant leap forward from the Mammoth. I also think Macklin Celebrini will be successful in dragging the Sharks to the playoffs in his third NHL season.

Nivison -- Columbus Blue Jackets: The Blue Jackets have been agonizingly close to the playoffs in each of the last two seasons, and I think they get over the hump in 2026-27. There are still questions in Columbus. Can Adam Fantilli be a franchise player at center? Is the forward group as a whole good enough to keep pace in a competitive Eastern Conference? Still, I am sure the Blue Jackets have a really strong blue line, led by Norris Trophy winner Zach Werenski, and goaltender Jet Greaves is on track to become a Vezina Trophy candidate. Internal improvements from the young core will then get Columbus above the cut line.

Baumgartner -- San Jose Sharks: The Sharks narrowly missed out on the 2026 Stanley Cup Playoffs, finishing just four points short of the second wild card. San Jose added a good group of veterans over the summer, but the most important offseason move was selecting Ivar Stenberg with the No. 2 pick in the Draft. Stenberg joins the youth movement in San Jose, which is spearheaded by new captain Macklin Celebrini, who broke the Sharks single-season points record with 115 last season. The Sharks are a better team than they were last year, and with Celebrini entering his third season as a legit Hart Trophy contender, this team won't be fun to play against.

Nivison: Yes, the Mammoth have a brutal path coming out of the Central Divison, but just close your eyes and imagine this scenario with me. Logan Cooley becomes a superstar center. Dylan Guenther hits 50 goals. Dmitry Simashev asserts himself as a budding top-four defenseman. Anders Lee and Vincent Trocheck provide necessary veteran depth. Now open your eyes. Utah is your Western Conference champion.

Unfortunately for the Mammoth, they will run into a refreshed Panthers team that now has double-barreled Tkachuks. Last season, we found out that all it takes to stop Florida is to hope all of its key players miss significant time with injury. The long offseason was probably a blessing in disguise as it allowed the Panthers to get healthy, and that's bad news for everyone else. The structure in front of the crease will limit some of the volatility we saw from Jacob Markstrom in New Jersey, and Florida wins its third Stanley Cup in four years.

Baumgartner: Before last season, the Carolina Hurricanes' kryptonite was the Eastern Conference Final. The Hurricanes were able to overcome their demons and win the East before ultimately taking home the franchise's first Stanley Cup since 2006. In the West, the Dallas Stars have been running into the same problem. After three straight seasons ending in the Western Conference Final, the Stars regressed last postseason, flaming out in the first-round to the Minnesota Wild. The Central Division will once again be a gauntlet, but I'm ready for Dallas to take the next step and reach the Stanley Cup Final.

While Dallas has continued to fall short in recent years, the Panthers have done the opposite. The Panthers made three consecutive Stanley Cup Final appearances, winning back-to-back Cups in 2023-24 and 2024-25. Last season, Florida's three-peat attempt came to a halt on day one of training after captain Aleksander Barkov went down with a non-contact injury, tearing both the ACL and MCL in his right knee. An offseason of healing for Barkov, and the rest of the banged up Panthers, has the team refreshed entering September for the first time in years. With nearly the entire 2025 Stanley Cup winning core still on the team and Brady Tkachuk added to the fold, Florida looks ready to win its third Stanley Cup in four seasons.

Nivison: Celebrini should have won the Hart Trophy last season, but for some incomprehensible reason, he wasn't even a finalist. This year, Celebrini replicates that performance and gets San Jose to the postseason to take home his first MVP award at age 20. Hughes posts a career year in his first full season with the Wild, and Spencer Carberry gets his flowers for winning the Metro Division after missing the playoffs last year.

Baumgartner: McDavid's ability to take over a game was evident nearly every time he touched the ice last season. His 24 points (11 goals,13 assists) in the final 14 games of the regular season -- without Leon Draisaitl in the lineup -- was one of the many reasons I put him No. 1 on my Hart Trophy ballot. With just two years left on his current contract, desperation may start to kick in to get the job in Edmonton, which would lead to another MVP-caliber season. Barkov is healthy and the frontrunner to win his fourth Selke, and Dahlin will have another strong season to take home his first career Norris Trophy.

#2774. MLB qualifying offer: Predicting who will get a QO this offseason, plus how the $23.15 million contract works

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Milwaukee Brewers have been crowned the 2026 World Series champions and the 2026-27 offseason is already underway. More than 100 players became free agents the day after the World Series ended, and soon teams will have to make decisions about contract options and qualifying offers.

The qualifying offer (QO) entitles teams to draft-pick compensation in the event that they lose a free agent to another team. The QO is a one-year deal set at the average of the top 125 salaries in baseball. This offseason, it's worth a record $23.15 million, according to the New York Post. That is up from $22.025 million last year, $21.05 million the year before, and $20.325 million the year before that.

Teams have until five days after the end of the World Series to tender their free agents the QO, and players who receive it then have until 4 p.m. ET on Nov. 17 to accept or reject. Players who accept the QO remain with their team and cannot be traded without their consent until June 15. Players who reject the QO become free agents with draft-pick compensation attached.

Simple, right? The process is, but the decisions aren't always. With that in mind, let's run down this offseason's QO candidates, as well as explain the draft-pick compensation rules.

Yes, the QO is still a thing this offseason. The collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1, and the next CBA could change the QO rules, maybe even eliminate it entirely. That said, until that happens, the QO remains in place. Decisions to tender the QO (made by the team) and decisions to accept or reject the QO (made by the player) are due before the CBA expires.

Once upon a time, teams that lost an eligible free agent received a compensation draft pick after the first round. It was nice and easy. The current rules are a bit more complicated. Here are compensation rules for teams that lose a qualified free agent:

Pick after competitive balance round B (before third round)

Pick after competitive balance round B (before third round)

The Athletics, Brewers, Cardinals, Diamondbacks, Guardians, Mariners, Marlins, Orioles, Pirates, Rays, Reds, Rockies, Royals, Tigers, and Twins received revenue sharing this season, so the first two scenarios apply to them. The Blue Jays, Braves, Cubs, Dodgers, Mets, Padres, Phillies, Red Sox, and Yankees will pay competitive balance tax (CBT), so they're in the third scenario. The Angels, Astros, Giants, Nationals, Rangers, and White Sox neither received revenue sharing nor paid CBT. They're in the fourth bucket.

Now here are the penalties for signing a qualified free agent:

The Blue Jays, Braves, Cubs, Dodgers, Mets, Padres, Phillies, Red Sox, and Yankees will pay CBT and are in the first group. The Athletics, Brewers, Cardinals, Diamondbacks, Guardians, Mariners, Marlins, Orioles, Pirates, Rays, Reds, Rockies, Royals, Tigers, and Twins received revenue sharing and are in the second group. The Angels, Astros, Giants, Nationals, Rangers, and White Sox are the third group. Got it? Good.

Thirteen players received the QO last offseason: Trent Grisham, Shota Imanaga, Gleyber Torres, and Brandon Woodruff accepted the QO; Zac Gallen, Michael King, and Kyle Schwarber declined but signed new contracts to remain with their teams; Bo Bichette, Dylan Cease, Edwin Díaz, Kyle Tucker, Ranger Suárez, and Framber Valdez rejected the QO and signed with new teams, giving their former clubs compensatory draft picks. Teams do not gain or lose draft picks for re-signing their own qualified free agent.

Players are eligible for the QO as long as they spent the entire 2026 season with one team and did not receive the QO previously. That means several high-profile free agents are not eligible for the QO this offseason. Here are the notables:

CHANGED TEAMS Luis Arraez Kevin Gausman (also received QO previously) Casey Mize Freddy Peralta Tarik Skubal Daulton Varsho

PREVIOUSLY RECEIVED QO Bo Bichette (opt out) Sonny Gray (mutual option) Michael King (opt out)  Nick Martinez

The Tigers traded Skubal, the reigning two-time AL Cy Young winner, to the Dodgers for a three-prospect package at the deadline. MLB Pipeline currently ranks those players as Detroit's No. 1 (Zyhir Hope), No. 3 (River Ryan), and No. 9 (Brady Smith) prospects. That's a much better haul than the compensation draft pick the Tigers would have received had they kept Skubal all year and made him the QO. Anyway, these free agents are among those not eligible for the QO this offseason.

This is not the best free agent class and, as a result, I count only two stone-cold locks to receive a QO: Randy Arozarena (Mariners) and Seiya Suzuki (Cubs). The Mariners and Cubs would be thrilled if Arozarena and Seiya accepted the QO and returned next season on one-year contracts that aren't too much of a raise. Arozarena made $15.65 million this year. Suzuki earned $18 million. The jump to $23.15 million isn't big enough to shy away from the QO, plus these are really good players. Arozarena and Suzuki will receive the QO and decline it.

Although Arozarena and Suzuki are the only locks to get the QO, in my opinion, there are three other free agents-to-be who seem like pretty good bets to receive it. Here are those three players:

Ryan Jeffers, Twins: Jeffers will be the best catcher to hit the open market since Willson Contreras four years ago. He missed time with a hamate injury this year and his defense isn't great, plus he'll turn 30 next June. Those seem like nitpicks compared to the offense he brings to the table at the catcher position. The only reason I don't think Jeffers is a lock to get the QO is the fact that the Twins have shaved roughly $50 million off their payroll the last four years. They might get thrifty.

Brandon Lowe, Pirates: Pittsburgh knocked it out of the park with the Mike Burrows-for-Lowe-and-Mason Montgomery three-team trade with the Astros and Rays. Montgomery is a bullpen ace and Lowe slugged 35 home runs, the most by a Pirate since Josh Bell hit 37 in 2019. Lowe's age (32), poor contact rates, and history of poor defense (though not in 2026) create collapse risk. Also, the Pirates run a bottom 10 payroll every season. I expect Lowe to get the QO. I just wouldn't be surprised if the Pirates decide not to risk him taking it, thereby soaking up 20% or so of their 2027 payroll.

Trevor Rogers, Orioles: Rogers, 29 in November, was a bright spot in an otherwise lost season for the O's. He stayed healthy and threw a career-high 169 ⅔ innings, and pitched exceptionally well after June 1: 2.90 ERA with under-the-hood numbers to match (2.89 FIP and 3.10 expected ERA). Rogers might be the second-best free agent starter behind Skubal given his success the last two years and (more importantly) analytically friendly arsenal. During the president of baseball operations Mike Elias era, the Orioles haven't always done the most sensible thing when it comes to spending money. I think it's 99% certain the O's will give Rogers the QO, but 99% is not 100%.

My hunch is teams will be conservative with their QO decisions this offseason because a new CBA is coming, and no one knows what the game's economic landscape will look like next year. Will there be a salary cap? More punitive CBT penalties? I would expect teams to err on the side of caution when it comes to potentially committing $23.15 million to one player. Even a good player they may want back, but not necessarily at $23.15 million in 2027. Here are three borderline QO cases:

David Bednar, Yankees: Bednar has proven he can close games in New York, which is not nothing, but he did just turn 32, and the $23.15 million QO would make him the highest-paid reliever in baseball. I think the Yankees want to bring Bednar back next season. Enough to risk him accepting the QO? When the potential reward is a dinky draft pick after the fourth round given their CBT status? That I'm not sold on. A multi-year contract at a lower annual salary is the much more likely path to Bednar returning to the Yankees.

Jazz Chisholm Jr., Yankees: Even in a down year, Chisholm was a 3.5-WAR player thanks to the breadth of his skill set. He hit 19 homers, he stole 41 bases, and he was fourth among second basemen with +13 outs above average. The all-around game and the fact that Chisholm will play the entire 2027 season at age 29 would seem to make him a slam dunk QO candidate. My sense is the Yankees won't commit any significant payroll to next season without first seeing what the new CBA brings, which is exactly what they did before the last lockout. I think the Yankees value the payroll flexibility (i.e. the certainty that Chisholm won't take the QO) more than the post-fourth round compensation pick they would receive if he signed elsewhere.

Adrian Morejon, Padres: Morejon will be an interesting test case for San Diego's new ownership. He is outstanding, one of the five or six best relievers in baseball, and he'll play the entire 2027 season at age 28. The QO would make Morejon the highest-paid reliever in the game, but only if he takes it, and his age and effectiveness would seem to make that unlikely. Do the Padres roll the dice and give Morejon the QO, and risk sinking $23.15 million into a (great) setup man, or not bother because they're only in line to receive a draft pick after the fourth round if he leaves? Díaz, Josh Hader (from the Padres), and Raisel Iglesias are the only relievers to get the QO in the last seven years. Is Morejon in that class?

#2767. 49ers Mailbag: Should the team get more defensive line help? What’s up with the return/kicking game?

What? You mean you guys like these things?

We haven't done too many mailbags this year, but maybe I can change that. Because of the timing, I wasn't able to get to every question asked in my call for submissions, but keep an eye out for the next one. I post over in the Niners Nation Feed when I'm going to do a mailbag, and I'll be sure to not do it on a Thursday this time. By the way, if you haven't gone to The Feed yet, what's stopping you? Not only am I there, but Fooch posts there a lot, too. Come hang out with the Niners Nation alum!

Now, as for this week, this is going up Saturday afternoon, and the San Francisco 49ers are preparing for the Las Vegas Raiders. This seems like another tricky game for the team. Raiders quarterback Kirk Cousins always seems to play well against the 49ers, like some long-standing grudge against Kyle Shanahan when the former was going to come in a few years before the latter traded for Jimmy Garoppolo. I think the 49ers can pull off the victory—based on the Raiders starting to remember they are the Raiders—but they can't make the same mistakes they did against the Atlanta Falcons.

If a Pontiac and a Buick both leave Chicago at the same time……….

They both will have engine failure two miles outside of city limits.

And keeping with the STs theme — why do they still have faith in Cowing returning punts? I'm terrified he's gonna drop it, even on a fair catch. If the former Ram who's on the practice squad isn't any better, why do we even have him on the team?

Probably because they don't want to pull from the very limited pool of wide receivers they already have and risk someone else getting beat up on the return game. I have to think that as the wide receivers come back, the 49ers move to…well…moving on from Cowing. At least at returner. They have Brandin Cooks on the roster, and while he's not as fast as he was a decade ago, he's still got some wheels and has been a returner in the past. De'Zhaun Stribling could also be a good option, but for reasons I just outlined, they may want him fresh for the offense and not on return duty because they aren't going to be able to rely on Mike Evans for every play.

I can't fathom a situation where Cowing is the punt returner in January based on what we've seen. This isn't even about his ball security issues; it's about his decision-making.

I'm of the mind that our D line is pretty awesome with Defo and Bosa on the field. My only reservation is injuries, especially Bosa. Do we really need to make a splash with an extra Edge? White, Williams and Height seems like a good rotation across from Bosa.

It could help, but I also think the 49ers need to hold onto some draft picks and salary cap space. Whoever they bring in, they have to make room for by releasing someone else, allocating what is the thinnest of margins in cap space, and sacrificing development of their younger talent. Not to mention draft picks. It's not the greatest answer, but when they bring in a Khalil Mack or some sort, that's going to take snaps away from a younger player who needs that experience and fewer picks to get more ammo in case that younger player doesn't work out.

I want to win now, just like all of you do, but not at the cost of development to stay competitive. I am not a fan of the Los Angeles' Rams way of just "buying" a Super Bowl for one year. Some players you know won't click; others need to be on the field and mess up, even in a championship season. The DeForest Buckner trade was great because while it removed snaps, it didn't do so much that it tossed the depth chart to the bench. Adding more could make things cramped. It also helped with the culture since Buckner has been there before and can be a good mentor

Speaking of which, that has already been paying dividends for young talent. Romello Height is getting up a bit earlier now, for one thing. The others have a lot to learn from Buckner as a player, and it's already rubbing off.

Has something changed in Piñeiro's mechanics, or with the snap and hold timing? Is he more accurate from one hash mark or another? How does he compare to the league average percentage of missed extra points? Why hasn't the team brought in another kicker for a tryout?

Why haven't they brought someone else in? Probably because Piñeiro just signed an extension with $10 million in guaranteed money. Kyle Shanahan did seem a bit miffed after the Atlanta game, but shortly after that, John Lynch affirmed the 49ers were sticking with Piñeiro. If you were wanting kicker tryouts—those aren't happening.

Have we hit David Akers or even Jake Moody levels of kicking? It's a rough patch, but I give him a couple more games. If he misses more XPs in the next two games, regardless of whether it's a victory or loss, the 49ers have to do something. It's just like if their punt returner had bad ball security and they did nothing…

Brandon Aiyuk owes the 49ers $13 million. If you'd signed that contract, what would you have spent the $13 million on?

I'd go to Vegas and make max bets on Casino War while getting bottle service. I'd set aside half for an executive suite at Levi's Stadium for one game. I'd also buy a sealed copy of Panzer Dragoon Saga for the Sega Saturn. If there's money leftover I'll also buy a gold cart of Nintendo World Championships.

#2766. Indiana Pacers Can Now Afford To Sign A Free Agent. Should They?

INDIANAPOLIS – The Indiana Pacers can now afford to sign a veteran 15th player to their roster. But do they need to do it right now?

That's the question the team's front office is considering. Entering the season, the Pacers team spending level was over the luxury tax line and, of all importance for their roster size, near the first apron. That first apron acts as a hard cap for Indiana because they used a specific salary cap exception to sign wing Kelly Oubre in the offseason.

When the season began, the Pacers had $206.8 million committed in terms of guaranteed contracts and possible salary bonuses. The first apron is just over $209 million. That left the team with a bit over $2.2 million in space between their roster spending and their hard cap.

The veteran's minimum for the entire 2026-27 NBA season is just shy of $2.45 million. That meant the Pacers couldn't even afford to sign a player to a minimum-salary agreement when the season began – only a player with zero (and drafted in the second round) or one year of service could have been added to their team at the time.

As a result, the Pacers carried 14 players on their roster to begin the season. But once the regular season starts, every passing day makes minimum contracts cheaper. They pro-rate based on how much of the season remains. And so earlier this week, a veteran's minimum contract became small enough in remaining value that the Pacers could afford to sign any available free agent to a one-year contract.

Entering the season, the answer to an early-as-possible addition seemed like it should be no. Just because the Pacers could sign someone doesn't mean they should. Because minimum contracts pro-rate, as noted above, every passing day gives the Pacers more flexibility. For example, if the team opted to sign a player on the first possible day they could have, and that player stayed with the team for the rest of the season, the Pacers (essentially) couldn't take back more salary than they sent out in trades or signed a player to a 10-day contract if they opened a roster spot – among many other transactions that would have become harder or impossible by using (basically) all of their remaining apron space at the first possible instant.

The Pacers can – if they're able to keep avoiding a signing – keep more team-building avenues open by waiting. Between slightly imbalanced trades, short-term signings, and other considerations related to their Mid-Level Exception, there are plenty of reasons to wait.

While that stance made good sense entering the season, things changed for the Pacers to start the campaign. T.J. McConnell went down with an injury early in training camp, and that was the first of many. Hamstring injuries stacked up. Guard Ben Sheppard is going to be out for a while. Others missed time. Indiana had just six players suit up in their loss against the Atlanta Hawks earlier this week.

With so many players down for the Pacers, the calculations changed. Do they need a player now just to survive their health situation? A 15th player could also open up a hardship contract slot down the line and would put a pause on the team's 90-game cap for their two-way contract signees while sitting on 14 players.

"I think it's fair to say that everything is on the table. We do need help," Pacers head coach Rick Carlisle said on Tuesday of this week during a radio appearance on 107.5 The Fan's Morning Show.

MEXICO CITY, MEXICO - NOVEMBER 06: Indiana Pacers player T.J. McConnell takes part in a practice session ahead of the NBA Mexico City Game between the Denver Nuggets and the Indiana Pacers, at Arena CDMX, in Mexico City, Mexico on November 06, 2026. (Photo by Daniel Cardenas/Anadolu via Getty Images)

Indiana has been hit hardest in the guard room. McConnell has yet to play this season, though that should change soon. Star ball handler Tyrese Haliburton is dealing with a hamstring injury. Andrew Nembhard missed two games with neck and back issues. Quenton Jackson hasn't missed a game but was sidelined early in camp.

That has put the team in a bind in the backcourt. Their wings and forward have stayed largely healthy, but some reserves have been inconsistent. That's even more true at center, where Jay Huff and Larry Nance Jr have taken on bigger roles after an injury to starter Ivica Zubac – though he has since returned.

In theory, the team could use an upgrade in the frontcourt, though the available free agents list isn't inspiring. And while a jolt of talent would be nice, with Zubac back and Obi Toppin an emergency option at center, the team is not in need of interior resources right now.

Haliburton and McConnell's absences make the need for a guard stronger for the Pacers. As recently as Monday, the team may have been more inclined to pursue free agent caretakers. But two things may have changed their thinking this week.

One is the return of McConnell to the lineup – he was able to practice in Mexico City recently and a brief assignment with the Pacers G League affiliate, the Noblesville Boom. The other is the emergence of Braden Smith, a point guard on a two-way contract who has risen his level of late and given the Pacers a lift at the point guard spot.

Because flexibility is so valuable to the Pacers, the emergence of Smith is a big deal. That, combined with recent returns to the lineup for McConnell and Zubac, makes putting off a signing logical despite more desperate times arriving last week.

"Everything is in play here," Carlisle said. "And if there's an opportunity to improve the team… Our [front office] will do it."

If Haliburton, Sheppard, and Johnny Furphy (torn ACL) are the only players sidelined for the Pacers, they can get by without a signing, and one would be unlikely in the short term. But the team is one or two more injuries away from needing more reinforcements. With November 5 in the rear view mirror, adding depth is a possibility if needed.

#2764. MLB rumors: Mets' Bo Bichette makes contract decision, familiar All-Star back on trade block

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026-27 MLB offseason is only two days old and already the hot stove moves and rumors are coming in. Here are our top 50 free agents and top 25 trade candidates, and here are the important offseason dates and deadlines you need to know. Here now are Friday's hot stove happenings.

As expected, Mets infielder Bo Bichette has picked up his $42 million player option for 2027, reports The Athletic. He holds another $42 million player option for 2028. Still only 28, Bichette had a poor first season in Queens, posting a .702 OPS with 18 home runs while showing growing pains as he transitioned from shortstop over to third base.

For now, the Mets are set on the infield with Bichette at third, Francisco Lindor at short, and Marcus Semien at second. They must figure out first base, and it is possible they will make a trade to shake up that veteran infield. Moving Semien would be ideal, but it may not be doable. Lindor's name figures to pop up in trade rumors against this offseason.

The Diamondbacks are expected to listen to offers for second baseman Ketel Marte, reports the Arizona Republic. The D-backs entertained trade offers last offseason, but were unable to find a match. Marte has full no-trade protection and can direct where he lands, if he wants to leave Arizona at all. His desire to change teams is unknown.

Marte, 33, had a down year by his standards in 2026. He also went AWOL in August, prompting the D-backs to put him on the restricted list. Manager Torey Lovullo later revealed it was the fourth straight season Marte missed a game without permission. Beyond the on-field fit, teams will have to weigh the potential clubhouse impact and headaches.

The Seibu Lions in Japan will make right-hander Kaima Taira available to MLB teams via the posting system this offseason, the team announced Friday. The posting is expected to be made official in the coming days. Once that happens, Taira will have 45 days to negotiate and sign with an MLB team, otherwise he will return to Japan in 2027.

We ranked Taira as the 19th-best free agent available this offseason. Here's our write-up:

Listed at 5-foot-8, Taira gets outlier extension down the mound (close to seven feet despite his height), which creates a low release window. Hitters rarely see the ball come from where Taira releases it. He's not a gimmick pitcher either. Taira sits mid-90s with his four-seam fastball and backs it up with a cutter, sinker, sweeper, slider, changeup, and splitter. The sweeper and slider are distinct pitches, as are the changeup and splitter. The Seibu Lions used Taira as a reliever in 2024 and 2025, then started him in 2026, and he handled the assignment well. The breaking balls are just OK, and the fact of the matter is that pitchers this height don't often hold up under a starter's workload. I would assume the team that signs Taira will give him a chance to start. In the long run, though, he might be a reliever, perhaps even a multi-inning setup man.

Taira, 27 next month, threw 146 innings with a 1.36 ERA and 141 strikeouts this past season. He actually had higher ERAs as a reliever in 2024 and 2025, though he has been excellent throughout his career in Japan, and has the bat-missing power stuff that tends to translate well to MLB. Taira figures to be highly sought after in the coming weeks.

The trading season resumed Thursday and the Red Sox were involved in the offseason's first two trades. First, they sent utility man Nate Eaton to the Athletics for minor-league righty Jareth Rayo, the team announced. The A's recently named former Red Sox assistant general manager Taylor Smith their new president of baseball operations. His first move was bringing in Eaton, a player he's presumably familiar with given their overlapping time in Boston.

Next, the Red Sox traded infielder Tsung-Che Cheng to the Tigers for cash, the team announced. Cheng, 25, is a glove-first utility man who appeared in 14 games with Boston this past season. Both the Cheng and Eaton trades open up 40-man roster spots for the Red Sox, who still must open three more spots to accommodate their seven players on the 60-day injured list. They must be activated no later than this coming Monday.

#2761. Maryland football survives late scare in 34-29 victory over Purdue

With Purdue down to a fourth-and-10 from their own 5-yard line and 44 seconds remaining, it appeared Maryland football's first Big Ten victory in 14 games was secured.

"They don't make it easy on me, man," interim head coach Aazaar Abdul-Rahim joked of his defense after the game.

Purdue found a completion to extend its two-minute drill, and it kept moving downfield, arriving at Maryland's 11-yard line with five seconds left.

But an illegal substitution pushed the offense back, giving Maryland's pass rush more time to deliver. And as quarterback Ryan Browne scrambled, Zion Elee spun him around, with Sidney Stewart delivering the leveling hit as time expired. The Terps held on to beat the Boilermakers, 34-29, for their first Big Ten win in 413 days.

The matchup between teams that each have just two Big Ten wins over the last three seasons looked the part early, with the Terps and the Boilermakers combining for 69 first-quarter yards.

Purdue got on the board first, kicking a field goal on a short drive after Bryce McFerson's punt went just 27 yards.

To start the second quarter, Maryland's linebackers lost wide receiver Asaad Waseem on a crossing route, and he peeled away for a 37-yard reception that set up another field goal.

Meanwhile, thanks to a Michael Hershey hands-in-the-face penalty that stalled out a promising drive, the Terps' first 16 offensive plays netted them 40 yards.

Maryland finally got past midfield with seven minutes to go in the first half, but that was because of an excellent kick return by Ricardo Cooper Jr.

After that special teams spark, the Terps' offense needed just three plays to reach the end zone. Malik Washington found Chris Durr Jr. in stride for a 31-yard gain before running in a 15-yard score off an option read.

Fortunately for the Terps, that touchdown cut the lead to two points. Maryland's defense bent to the tune of 156 second-quarter yards, but it refused to break, holding the Boilermakers to field goals on each of their first three red zone drives.

After another Purdue field goal, Maryland's two-minute drive was cut short by an incomprehensible interception — Washington's pass hit Dorian Fleming's ready hands and flew into the air for an easy pick.

Purdue couldn't capitalize, though. Elee sacked the quarterback on a crucial third down, pushing the Boilermakers back into a Hail Mary — where the freshman got home again to erase the turnover.

Following the half, Maryland had four straight touchdowns, finding the scoring groove that had evaded it all season.

The Terps' offense earned its first second-half score, grinding over midfield before Na'eem Abdul-Rahim Gladding burst free from a crowded set for a 44-yard score. The second came from a piece of defensive fortune.

Lavain Scruggs got into the backfield and stripped quarterback Ryan Browne, with the Terps recovering on the two-yard line. But on three tries, the run game struck out.

Washington, rushed back onto the field with an injured knee, took matters into his own hands. Receiving the fourth-down snap under center, Washington rose up, cresting over his offensive line to reach the ball into the end zone.

Purdue got a touchdown back, courtesy of some big plays that moved the chains. But DeJuan Williams responded with an even bigger play, running 75 yards untouched into the end zone on the offense's first snap back on the field.

Maryland's defense again held strong in the red zone, forcing the Boilermakers to kick a field goal after having first-and-goal three yards out.

Purdue almost immediately paid for coming short. Cooper scampered away on another kickoff, this time reaching the end zone. However, a block in the back by Jayden Kitchens nullified the score, bringing Maryland back to the 12-yard line.

Durr, who had cooled off through October after a fiery start to the season, had a piece of individual brilliance to give the Terps just enough cushion. Catching a screen deep in the left flat, the Wyoming transfer sliced through the entire defense, climbing the ladder to the right sideline and sprinting to the end zone for an 87-yard score.

Purdue cut the score with a 13-play, 75-yard drive, and it fended off the Terps' offense around midfield to earn one more possession. Ultimately, though, Maryland's red zone defense came out on top.

1. Backfield pressure wins the game. The Terps finished Saturday's game with seven sacks, their most since 2020, and a season-high 13 total tackles for loss. Alongside Elee and his 2.5 sacks, Nahsir Taylor, Trey Reddick and CJ Smith each had multiple tackles for loss.

2. Punting battle lost. McFerson has struggled in 2026 — the preseason Ray Guy watch list punter's 42.21 yard per punt average entering Saturday was second-worst in the Big Ten. With Maryland needing to scrap for field position against the Boilermakers, McFerson's first two punts went for a combined 62 yards. But the senior finally had a short punt go his way, pinning Purdue at the 5-yard line for its final drive.

3. Terps lost their tempers. Five plays into the game, embattled cornerback Dontay Joyner was ejected. Referees determined he threw a punch; three plays earlier, he had also thrown a slap at an opponent. Joyner's was one of nine Maryland penalties on the afternoon.

Emotions remained at a simmer throughout. Messiah Delhomme, DD Holmes and Elee scuffled along the Boilermakers' sideline in the third quarter; only Elee escaped without a personal foul, but none were ejected. The trio continued to make plays to seal the game.

#2760. Astros hire Randy Flores as new general manager as offseason filled with questions begins in Houston

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Houston Astros' search for a new head of baseball operations has ended with the hiring of Randy Flores as general manager. The 51-year-old Flores had been an assistant general manager with the St. Louis Cardinals. In Houston, Flores replaces Dana Brown, who was let go in late August. Flores becomes the fourth head of baseball operations to serve under Astros owner Jim Crane.

"Randy has had a huge impact on the Cardinals over the last 10 seasons," Crane said in a statement released by the club. "Throughout the entire interview process, we've been thoroughly impressed with Randy and his background in scouting and player acquisition. We're happy to welcome Randy and his family to the Astros and we can't wait to get to work on bringing another championship to Houston."

Added Flores: "I am excited and grateful for this amazing opportunity. The Astros have a long winning tradition under Jim Crane, and I look forward to contributing to the success.  I want to thank the Cardinals organization for the opportunities and support that made this next chapter possible. My family and I are excited to make Houston home."

Flores for roughly a decade served as scouting director for the Cardinals and was tasked with running their draft. He added the assistant GM title in 2018 and saw his portfolio of responsibilities expand within the last year.

Flores takes over an Astros organization beset by uncertainty. With an aging roster and after several key departures over the years, the Astros have seen their season-long win total decline for four straight years. This past season, the Astros eked out the American League Central title but finished with a .500 record and a negative run differential. In terms of success and roster strength, they're a long way from their dynasty years of 2017-22. It's not certain whether the Astros moving forward will try to squeeze out another season of relevance or embrace a rebuild, but either path will have its challenges.

Speaking of challenges, Crane and his trusted advisor Jeff Bagwell have been an increasingly meddlesome presence in recent years, and it's unclear to what degree Flores will have autonomy in his role. Whatever the future holds, Flores' first major decision is filling the managerial vacancy. After the end of the regular season, Crane opted not to renew the contract of former manager Joe Espada.

Prior to beginning his front office career, Flores spent parts of eight seasons in the majors as a left-handed reliever. In 2006, he earned a World Series ring as a member of that Cardinals team.

#2759. Alexander Ovechkin announces this will be his last NHL season: 'Let's have fun'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Alex Ovechkin's 22nd NHL season will be his last, the Washington Capitals superstar announced on Monday."This is gonna be my last year," Ovechkin told his teammates in a video the Capitals posted to social media. "It's sad, but it is what it is. We have an unbelievable team this year. There are 82 games left. Let's make the playoffs, and let's have fun."

Ovechkin has already established himself as the greatest goal-scorer in hockey history with 929 tallies, and he still has 82 games to add to that total before he hangs up his skates.

The No. 1 overall pick in the 2004 NHL Draft, Ovechkin immediately established himself as a prolific scorer by notching 52 goals en route to winning the Calder Trophy as a rookie.

Since then, Ovechkin has won the Rocket Richard Trophy as the NHL's leading goal-scorer a record nine times. The Capitals legend's resume also features an Art Ross Trophy and three Hart Trophy wins.

The crowning achievement in Ovechkin's illustrious career is leading Washington to its first Stanley Cup in 2017-18. After coming up short in a number of postseasons prior to that, Ovechkin led all playoff performers with 15 goals and won the Conn Smythe Trophy as a result.

Following the 2025-26 season, there was speculation that Ovechkin could retire, but he signed an incentive-laden one-year deal with the Caps.Sensing that this could be Ovechkin's final season, the Capitals loaded up to give their franchise icon one more shot at the Stanley Cup. Washington signed former Buffalo Sabres winger Alex Tuch in free agency and acquired winger Jordan Kyrou from the St. Louis Blues via trade.

No team is as loaded on the wings as the Capitals, and they have one of the best rosters in the Metro Division. Washington has the ingredients to challenge the defending Cup champion Carolina Hurricanes and get Ovechkin one more ring before he rides off into the sunset.

#2758. Paderborn vs. Eintracht Frankfurt preview: Die Adler searching for third successive win

Competing in the top flight for the first time since 2019-20, Paderborn are sitting in 14th spot after winning two, drawing three and losing three of their eight league games. The second of those victories came in their most recent home outing, a 1-0 success over Hamburger SV on October 24.

However, they have failed to score since Rayan Philippe netted an 88th-minute winner against Hamburg. They fell to a 1-0 defeat to Stuttgart in the DFB-Pokal, before they played out a goalless draw in last Saturday’s away clash against Borussia Mönchengladbach.

While the goals have dried up, Paderborn can at least be pleased with the fact they have avoided defeat in each of their last three league games (W1, D2). However, the league’s second-lowest scorers know they will need to improve in the final third if they are to put distance between themselves and the drop zone, with Ralf Kettemann’s side currently sitting two points clear of the bottom three.

They can take some confidence from the fact they have won all three of their previous home meetings with Frankfurt, even if the most recent of those encounters took place nearly seven years ago in December 2019.

Mario Götze is unlikely to feature due to an ear infection, denying him the chance to face off against his brother Felix Götze. Hütter is also without Jessic Ngankam, while Robin Koch is a doubt due to a knee problem.

Frankfurt head into the weekend in eighth spot after winning three, drawing two and losing three of their eight Bundesliga matches. Die Adler took maximum points from last Sunday’s home clash against Hamburger SV, just a matter of days after beating the same opponent by the same 3-1 scoreline in the DFB-Pokal.

The league encounter was level at one goal apiece at half time before Raphael Onyedika and Younes Ebnoutalib found the net to fire Adi Hütter’s side to all three points. After enjoying a successful outing at Deutsche Bank Park, Frankfurt will now head on their travels with the minimum objective of avoiding a third consecutive away defeat in the Bundesliga.

Their ultimate goal will be to record their second away win of the season, although that would require them to beat Paderborn at the Home Deluxe Arena for the very first time. While a head-to-head away win has evaded them up until this point, they were victorious in the most recent meeting between the two sides in June 2020, when they held off a Paderborn fightback to clinch a 3-2 win.

The visitors are expected to be without Marcel Hoffmeier, Nyamekye Awortwie-Grant and Timur Gayret. In positive news, Sven Michel is available for selection after recovering from the injury that has kept him out of the last two matches.

#2757. MLB rumors: Padres decline option on key rotation piece, Korean star to be posted

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026-27 MLB offseason is only four days old and already the hot stove moves and rumors are coming in. Here are our top 50 free agents and top 25 trade candidates, and here are the important offseason dates and deadlines you need to know. Here now are Sunday's hot stove happenings.

San Diego's top two starters are now free agents. Two days after Michael King exercised an opt-out clause to become a free agent, the Padres declined their $14 million club option on Nick Pivetta, reports the San Diego Union-Tribune. Had the Padres picked up the option, Pivetta would have held an $18 million player option for 2028. That surely factored into the team's decision.

Pivetta, 34 in February, missed roughly five months with a flexor strain this past season. He returned late in the season and pitched reasonably well in six starts spanning September and the postseason. The San Diego Union-Tribune notes the Padres still have concerns about Pivetta's elbow, but could re-sign him to a new contract with a lower salary and/or no player option.

San Diego signed Pivetta to what amounted to a two-year, $23 million contact with two players options in February 2025. The flexor strain triggered an injury clause that converted the 2027 player option into a club option. We ranked Pivetta as the offseason's 43rd-best free agent.

As expected, the Orioles have declined their $20 million club option for center fielder Luis Robert Jr., reports ESPN. They will pay him a $2 million buyout, so it was functionally an $18 million decision. Robert suffered a hamstring injury and played only three games with the O's after being claimed off waivers from the Mets in late September.

Now 29, Robert again had multiple stints on the injured list this past season. He continued to punish lefties and play solid center field defense when healthy, but injuries have limited him to only 271 of 489 possible regular-season games from 2024-26. We did not rank Robert among our top 50 free agents, though he is an interesting upside play given his age.

The Hanwha Eagles of the Korea Baseball Organization will post star third baseman Si-Hwan Roh for MLB teams this offseason, reports Yonhap News Agency. Roh signed the richest deal in KBO history in February (11 years and $23 million), though as part of the deal, the Eagles agreed to post him this offseason, and Roh agreed to return to the team once his MLB stint is over.

Roh, 26, has been one of the KBO's best players the last several years. He hit .283/.360/.505 with 29 home runs in 2026, and has averaged 35 home runs per 162 games since 2023. Roh is considered a reliable but unspectacular defender at third, plus he has first base experience as well. This free agent class is very thin at the hot corner. Roh should generate a good deal of interest.

KBO players get a 30-day negotiating window once officially posted. If Roh does not sign with an MLB team during the 30-day window, he will return to the Eagles. It's possible that Roh, a right-handed hitter, will eclipse his $23 million guarantee with the Eagles over just a handful of years with an MLB team.

The Astros have acquired Triple-A righty reliever Evan Reifert from the Rays for cash, reports the Tampa Bay Times. Houston is likely to add him to their 40-man roster to protect him from the Rule 5 Draft. The Rays did not have the roster space to do that, so they traded for cash rather than lose him for nothing. Reifert, 27, has an excellent slider and used it to strike out 81 batters in 58 Triple-A innings in 2026. He should spend time in Houston's bullpen next season.

New York Mets team Hall of Famer and two-time All-Star Jerry Koosman died Sunday morning in Osceola, Wisconsin, the team announced. He was 83. The Mets say Koosman battled multiple illnesses before his death.

"Kooz was one of the greatest pitchers in team history and a beloved member of the Mets family," Mets owners Alex and Steve Cohen said in a statement. "The 1969 Miracle Mets were filled with heroes, and the special southpaw from Appleton, Minnesota, was central to their success. He was a fierce competitor on the field, and respected teammate in the clubhouse. His legendary performance in the World Series helped the Mets secure their first Championship in team history. On behalf of the entire Mets organization, we extend our heartfelt condolences to Jerry's family, friends, former teammates and all who loved him."

The Mets discovered Koosman while he was pitching for the United States Army and signed him to a contract in August 1964. He made his MLB debut in April 1967 and moved into the rotation full-time the next season. Koosman threw 263 ⅔ innings with a 2.08 ERA as a rookie in 1968, which earned him an All-Star Game selection and MVP votes, and a second-place finish in the Rookie of the Year voting behind Hall of Famer Johnny Bench.

In 1969, Koosman was again an All-Star, throwing 241 innings with a 2.28 ERA. He was New York's No. 2 starter in the postseason between Hall of Famers Tom Seaver and Nolan Ryan. Koosman made two starts for the Miracle Mets in the World Series, including the Game 5 clincher against the Baltimore Orioles. He allowed three runs in the complete game win and recorded all but one possible out in his two World Series starts.

From 1968-76, Koosman was simply one of the best pitchers in the game, pitching to a 2.94 ERA and averaging 223 innings per season. The Mets traded him to the Minnesota Twins for Jesse Orosco in December 1978 and Koosman finished his career with stints for the Twins (1979-81), Chicago White Sox (1981-83), and Philadelphia Phillies (1984-85).

Koosman retired following the 1985 season with a 222-209 record and a 3.36 ERA that is 39th among AL/NL pitchers with at least 3,500 career innings. He ranks 35th all-time in strikeouts (2,556), 40th all-time in starts (527), 48th all-time in innings (3,839 ⅓), and 77th all-time in pitching WAR (57.0). Koosman went to two All-Star Games and finished second to Randy Jones in the 1976 Cy Young voting.

The Mets inducted Koosman into their Hall of Fame in 1989 and retired his No. 36 in 2021. His 140 wins are the most in franchise history among left-handers and third in team history overall, behind Seaver (198) and Dwight Gooden (157). Koosman is second in Mets history in innings (behind Seaver) and third in strikeouts (behind Seaver and Gooden).

Koosman fell off the Baseball Writers Association of America's Hall of Fame ballot in 1991, his first year of eligibility.

The winners of the 2026 Rawlings Gold Glove were announced Sunday night by Major League Baseball and, as expected, Cubs wunderkind Pete Crow-Armstrong took home his second straight National League Gold Glove in center field. PCA, who also won a Gold Glove in 2025 and is expected to be named the NL MVP in 2026, was the best defender in baseball this past season based on both the numbers and the eye test.

Here are the game's best defenders in 2026 according to Statcast's Fielding Runs Value, an all-encompassing metric that factors in range and arm, as well as blocking and framing for catchers:

Crow-Armstrong's +26 FRV is the fifth best in a single season since FRV launched in 2016 and the second best by a non-catcher, trailing only Nick Ahmed's +28 FRV season at shortstop in 2018.

Gold Gloves have be awarded since 1957 and are given to the best defensive player at each position in each league. That first year was one MLB-wide honor at each position. In 1958, Gold Gloves were split into AL and NL. Also, it used to be three outfielders per league regardless of exact position. Now the outfield spots are broken down into left field, center field, and right field.

Winners are determined through manager/coach voting (75%) and a statistical component (25%). Team employees can not vote for their own players.

While MLB announced "finalists" for each Gold Glove a few weeks back, remember that the voting was already complete and those finalists were simply the top three vote-getters at each position. This means, obviously, that postseason performance had no impact. Here now are the 2026 Gold Glove winners.

#2748. Dolphins surprisingly healthy heading into Week 9 with Lions missing starters

The Miami Dolphins are heading into their Week 9 game against the Detroit Lions surprisingly healthy for a mid-season game. The Dolphins listed only three players on their final injury report on Friday, and all three were questionable at worst. Miami will likely have its entire roster available for the game.

The Lions, meanwhile, ruled out five players, all starters. for the game. They also had three players listed as questionable.

Rookie guard Kadyn Proctor cleared concussion protocol after missing last week's game against the New England Patriots. Proctor's return to the lineup returns the Dolphins to their original starting lineup with left tackle Patrick Paul, left guard Proctor, center Aaron Brewer, right guard Jonah Savaiinaea, and right tackle Austin Jackson.

On Friday, The Phinsider's Marek Brave wrote, "In [Proctor's] absence, Miami's offensive line struggled against a stout Patriots front — allowing 5 sacks and managing just 74 yards rushing on 20 attempts (just 3.7 yards per carry)." Getting Proctor back into the lineup should assist the Dolphins as they face the ninth-ranked rush defense in the league on Sunday.

Dolphins quarterback Malik Willis, who was a full participant all week in practice, has been dealing with a groin injury for the last couple of week. He was asked this week if the injury led to a reluctance to run last week against the Patriots and he was pretty straight forward that they were not connected. "I think that's just how the game played out. I'm not sure that had anything to do with it really," he stated.

Willis continued to be listed on the injury report this week with the injury, but was not given a game-day status, indicating he will be starting.

The Lions have not been as lucky with their injuries. Linebacker Jack Campbell, who sustained a serious neck injury early in last week's game against the Minnesota Vikings, was obviously going to be ruled out of the game. Several other players were also given the "out" designation.

Safety Kerby Joseph continues to work his way back from the physically unable to perform list with a knee injury. According to Pride of Detroit's Erik Schlitt, the Lions plan on ramping up Joseph's workload next week. He has a little over a week remaining on his practice window before the team has to move him to the 53-man roster or leave him on the PUP for the remainder of the year.

Center Cade Mays has an ankle injury and the Lions have been preparing for him to be out this weekend. Juice Scruggs will start in his place.

Cornerback D.J. Reed has a hip injury and has not been able to practice all week.

Edge rusher DJ Wonnum has a concussion and is working his way through the protocols.

Including Joseph, who will move into the starting lineup once he is activated off the PUP, all five players are starters for the Lions.

The biggest injury concerns for the Dolphins heading into this weekend's game may be at running back depth. While Ollie Gordon II, elevated to the starting role after De'Von Achane's season-ending injury early this year, will see most snaps, both Jaylen Wright and Kaytron Allen are questionable for the game. While they will likely both be available, Miami's depth may be fairly shallow if anything aggravates the quadriceps injuries nagging both players. Wright did not practice on Wednesday before being limited on both Thursday and Friday; Allen was limited for the first two days before being a full participant on Friday.

Miami also listed edge rusher Malik Herring as questionable with a neck injury. He was limited in practice all week.

#2747. MLB Power Rankings: Brewers end 2026 season at No. 1 as World Series champions

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

I'm done. No more. Enough is enough. I have doubted the Brewers far too many times and I decided in early August to never do it again. I started picking them to win the World Series every chance I got. I was finally right.

Every time they traded away someone good (the latest being Freddy Peralta last offseason), I thought, "OK, now is when it finally catches up with them." Only it never does. I thought they needed Tarik Skubal, both to reinforce their rotation and also to keep him away from the Dodgers. It didn't matter. They beat him and swept the Dodgers in the NLCS.

It's a juggernaut of an organization. They churn out talent and get the most out of every player they have. They seem to trade away talent at the exact right time. They develop young stars better than anyone. There's another one coming in Jesús Made, but there's no reason for Brewers fans to dream about the future when the present is World Series champions.

Jackson Chourio is becoming a superstar, Jacob Misiorowski is going to win the National League Cy Young and Christian Yelich is a former MVP, but it isn't really about the big names with this group. It's everything. It's the entire team making this train run, working as a cohesive unit. It's Robert Gasser going out and dealing in Game 3 after starting the season in the minors. It's Jake Bauers winning NLCS MVP not too long after he was ready to retire from baseball. It's Aaron Ashby putting up one of the greatest reliever performances in playoff history. It's Sal Frelick hitting a game-tying bomb. It's Cooper Pratt's coming-out party in the World Series. And on and on and on we could go.

Milwaukee is the best organization in baseball now, supplanting the former two-time defending champion Dodgers.

The Brewers head to next season with plenty of question marks, but they'll answer them. They always do. They are the champions of Major League Baseball and they sit atop the final 2026 Power Rankings.

Looking forward to next spring, my expectation is the Brewers will be No. 1. Some years, I write about why the defending champion is not No. 1. I've long since learned my lesson with this team, though. No more. The Brewers will be No. 1 heading into spring training.

I hate to get so negative just one week into the season, but the Philadelphia Flyers have forced my hand. After a magical run to the second round of the 2026 Stanley Cup Playoffs, the Flyers have fallen on their face through four games.

The Flyers are off to an 0-2-2 start, and the underlying numbers aren't pretty. Per Natural Stat Trick, they have a five-on-five expected goals share of 26.0%, which ranks last in the NHL. Their 4.57 xGA/60 also ranks last. Their 1.94 xGF/60? You guessed it. Last.

Rookie Porter Martone asserted himself as a budding star with six goals and nine assists in 19 games between the regular season and playoffs.

There's still plenty of time -- 80 games exactly -- for the Flyers to get back on track and restore that optimism, but to say this has been a discouraging start would be an understatement.

#2743. LaNorris Sellers injury update: South Carolina QB leaves Texas A&M game for locker room

LaNorris Sellers left South Carolina's game against Texas A&M on Saturday, Nov. 7, with an apparent injury.

The star quarterback left during the second quarter after taking a sack and fumbling, injuring his ankle. He left the field and briefly entered the injury tent before entering the locker room with a trainer.

"We're concerned, he's got an ankle right now," South Carolina coach Shane Beamer told ESPN at halftime. "Taking an X-ray on it, don't know the results of that right now."

The third-year starter has been fantastic during the Gamecock's 3-game win streak and is coming off a 5-touchdown performance in a 42-25 rout of Oklahoma in Week 9. Sellers entered the game with 1,849 passing yards and 22 total touchdowns to seven interceptions.

Losing Sellers would be a huge blow to Beamer's squad, especially with South Carolina play some of the best football in the SEC as of late.

"We have a lot of confidence in Cutter Woods," Beamer said. "He's our backup. Total confidence in him. The bigger issue right now is we're getting our butts kicked on the line of scrimmage. We're not running the ball and they're running the ball down our throats right now."

Sellers left the game against Texas A&M in the second quarter with an ankle injury after being sacked. He briefly entered the injury tent on the sideline before entering the locker room with a trainer.

Beamer said Sellers is getting x-rays on his ankle, but that the team is concerned about his status.

#2738. Rangers lose star goaltender Igor Shesterkin for season with lower-body injury; what's next for New York?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Rangers goaltender Igor Shesterkin will miss the remainder of the season with a lower-body injury, the team announced on Saturday.

Shesterkin suffered an apparent leg injury in the Rangers' loss to the Washington Capitals on Friday night as his right leg slid awkwardly into the post while scrambling to get back in position. Shesterkin fell to the ice immediately, and he needed assistance to get down the tunnel.

Prior to that loss, the Rangers were off to a terrific 4-1-0 start, and Shesterkin was a driving force behind that success. In just five appearances, Shesterkin posted 3.90 goals saved above average with a .900 high-danger save percentage, according to Natural Stat Trick.

The 2022 Vezina Trophy winner, Shesterkin has put up sparkling numbers since he entered the NHL in 2019-20. In 330 games, Shesterkin boasts a .917 save percentage, a 2.51 GAA and 22 shutouts. Over the last three full seasons from 2023-26, Shesterkin ranked third in goals saved above average with 45.4. Only Connor Hellebuyck and Andrei Vasilevskiy were better in that category.

Shesterkin was a big reason why the Rangers felt they could bounce back from a disappointing 2025-26 season, and losing the star goaltender puts a huge dent in the team's playoff hopes. It doesn't help that backup goalie Joonas Korpisalo is also hurt.

Dylan Garand replaced Shesterkin on Friday night, and Spencer Martin will be recalled from the AHL after recovering from his own injury. With the Rangers playing well early, it wouldn't be a shock to see them explore better replacement options for Shesterkin.

New York won't be able to replace Shesterkin's impact because he's one of the five best goalies in the world. However, the team should be able to upgrade its current goaltending situation, which is a fairly low bar to clear.

First, there are unsigned veterans still on the open market in Petr Mrazek and James Reimer. Neither one was great last season -- hence their availability at the moment -- Reimer and Mrazek could provide a level of stability in the crease that the Rangers simply don't have right now.

New York could also explore trade possibilities, and Minnesota Wild netminder Filip Gustavsson could be a solution there. Jesper Wallstedt is the future of the crease in Minnesota, making Gustavsson more of a luxury. Would the Wild send Gustavsson to New York in exchange for some draft capital it could use to acquire a center?

The one snag in a potential Gustavsson deal is his contract. Gustavsson is in the first year of a deal that pays him $6.8 million over the next five seasons. That's a big commitment for a player who will become a backup when Shesterkin returns.

Obviously, Connor Hellebuyck has been on the trade market for months now, but that trade wouldn't make sense for the Rangers. Hellebuyck is on an expensive long-term deal, and New York would have $20 million tied up in goalies if they made that move, not to mention the astronomical acquisition cost.

However, if you'll allow me to get creative here, it's no secret that the Florida Panthers have pursed Hellebuyck. What if the Panthers traded Jacob Markstrom -- just acquired in the offseason -- to the Rangers in order to make room for Hellebuyck?

Markstrom does have a 20-team no-trade list, so the question is whether New York would be one of his 11 approved teams. Florida flipping Markstrom so quickly seems like a long shot, but the team has taken plenty of big swings in recent history.
